#1036. Germany's celebrated children's author Janosch has died

Bear, Tiger and Tiger-Duck: The author and illustrator Janosch achieved world fame with his heartwarming children's figures. He died at the age of 95.

Janosch, the pen name of German author and illustrator Horst Eckert, won hearts around the world with his warm and simple sense of humor. He charmed children and adults alike with his iconic Tiger, Bear, Tiger-Duck and other animals.

Janosch created more than 150 books, which have been translated into over 30 languages.

His best-selling children's book, "Oh, wie schön ist Panama," translated into English as "The Trip to Panama," was so lucrative that Janosch was able to settle down on the Canary Island of Tenerife in 1980, where he lived together with his wife Ines. The writer and illustrator died peacefully at the age of 95, his publisher Bernhard Feil announced on Wednesday.

Janosch was born as Horst Eckert on March 11, 1931, in Hindenburg (now Zabrze, Poland) in what was then Upper Silesia. After World War II, his family had to flee to Germany.

In 1953, Janosch started studying at the Academy of Art in Munich, thinking that it would be easy to become an artist. He was however dismissed after just a few terms for "lack of talent."

But luckily for his later readers, Janosch did not give up. He continued to work as a freelance artist, soon discovering his second great gift, namely writing.

His first children's book about a horse named Valek was published in 1960.

Although Janosch became famous primarily for his children's books, he also wrote books for adults that focused on his own childhood.

Even though he wrote cheerful books for children, Janosch hardly had any positive memories of his own childhood, as his father was an alcoholic. He was beaten not only by him but also by his mother and grandmother. Raised in a strictly Catholic environment, he was continuously threatened to be punished by God.

Later on, Janosch tried to overcome the burden of his childhood memories by turning to alcohol as well.

He always expressed a great deal of understanding for children, trying to encourage them to stand up for their rights. As a result of his childhood experiences, Janosch did not want to have children himself, and his attitude towards the Catholic Church always remained divided. "As I am a sinner and a heretic, God will let me live a long life so that I can return to the Church," he told his biographer Angela Bajorek.

Janosch's animal figures are endearing but not always well-behaved. They love all kinds of nonsense. But even if they lie to each other or put their own interests first, the true winner at the end of stories is always friendship and solidarity.

Janosch achieved his major breakthrough with "The Trip to Panama," a story about two friends, a little tiger and a bear, who set out to find their paradise in Panama. After touring around in circles, they finally end up where they started out; they realize that their journey was the destination. Janosch received the German Youth Book Prize in 1979 for the work.

Janosch's protagonists have become familiar to generations of children all over the world. They come up over and over again in the various stories carefully illustrated with water colors.

There is the honest lion Hans from the toy chest who fails to catch a nutcracker with his lies. There is Schnuddel and a ridiculous bragger Günter the Box-Frog. And then there is a tiger that collects mushrooms while looking out for his devoted friend, a bear, who always stands up for him even when the tiger temporarily leaves him because of a little pig in one of the stories.

The "Tigerente," literally "Tiger-Duck," a wooden duck on wheels with yellow-brown stripes, appears on numerous pictures by the illustrator. At times, the animal has been tossed into a corner, at times it is hanging from the ceiling, or the Box-Frog pulls it across the drawing.

His iconic figures, especially the Tiger-Duck, have served as motifs on various items, from cups to stamps to jewelry, and even on airplanes. Film adaptations and TV series based on his stories were produced in German and English.

Guests who visited Janosch in Tenerife were impressed by his very modest lifestyle. He always said that hanging around in his hammock doing nothing was what he enjoyed most. And yet Janosch remained very active until the end of his life.

From 2013 to 2019, he wrote a column for the German weekly Die Zeit, taking on the role of Mr. Wondrak, who commented on world affairs. Shortly before his 90th birthday in 2021, the complete collection of his Mr. Wondrak columns were published as a book in German.

Like the protagonists in his stories, Janosch always tried to content himself with few things. As he wrote in one of his books: "He who needs almost nothing, has everything."

This article was originally written in German.

Brazilian winger Willian enjoyed a successful career in English football, turning out more than 400 times for Chelsea, Arsenal and Fulham,

During this time, he established himself as one of the Premier League’s most exciting attackers, most notably at Stamford Bridge, where he won two league titles, an FA Cup, a League Cup and the Europa League.

After enjoying success at Shakhtar Donetsk, where he won five Ukrainian Premier League titles in a six-season spell, Willian was snapped up by the ambitious Anzhi.

“I wanted a new challenge [after Shakhtar] and Anzhi had very big ambitions. As well as Eto’o, Lassana Diarra was also there,” the Brazilian tells FourFourTwo.

But when the club’s ailing owner withdrew his financial backing, the project faced an uncertain future.

“But I ended up staying for only six months as, unfortunately, the owner had some health problems and decided he wouldn't invest in the club any more. So he sold all the players he had invested in, and that's why I left.”

Using London as a base, Willian began negotiations with a host of clubs as he looked to resolve his future.

But while Spurs pushed especially hard to sign the former Corinthians youngster, Willian had his heart set elsewhere.

Roy Keane accused visiting Manchester United supporters at Anfield of “applauding rubbish” after Liverpool romped to a 4-0 win.

Mauricio Pochettino’s first game in charge got off to the worst possible start when Leny Yoro was red-carded after eight minutes.

Dominik Szoboszlai and Florian Wirtz made it 2-0 to Liverpool inside 13 minutes, after which United’s 10 men never looked like responding.

Two goals in the second half from Rio Ngumoha and Victor Munoz further laid bare the size of the task facing Pochettino as United were left second-bottom of the Premier League.

Some travelling fans offered encouraging applause to the players at the end, a reflection of perhaps of the losing cause they had fought after losing Yoro so early but, speaking on Sky Sports, Keane suggested it was a mark of how low standards have fallen.

“Has a team ever got a result before with 10 men? It can be done,” he said, taking issue with a comment made by Gary Neville highlighting the importance of the red.

“Are you telling me Man Utd couldn’t have done better and everyone is saying it’s not bad. At least show a bit more fight, a bit more quality, I can’t believe what I’m hearing.

“Fans are applauding the players, applauding what? Applauding rubbish. When do the players take responsibility for some of the decision-making? Liverpool should have scored eight or nine.

“I feel like swearing. How can anyone say 4-0 is not too bad?”

Keane fumed over United’s failure to get the basics right on a dire afternoon, with Matthijs de Ligt in particular struggling in his first league start in over a year.

"If you do the basics right, you give yourself a bit of a chance so no matter how good you think you might be or a big club you are, if you're not doing the basics right, you're going to be constantly under pressure and constantly getting criticised,” he added.

"If that happened against a pub team, they'd be criticising you and this is a big game.

"You're talking about starting well, being solid, but again, we go back to the defensive shape and one stray ball over the top puts somebody in on goal.

#1031. ‘Sacked in the morning’: Mauricio Pochettino taunted by Liverpool fans during catastrophic Man Utd bow

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Pochettino started life as Man United manager with a 4-0 hammering at the hands of Liverpool

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The job of Manchester United head coach has become something of a poisoned chalice for a succession of managers but even new boss Mauricio Pochettino could not have expected how quickly he would be taunted with jokes about him being sacked.

His reign began in humiliating fashion after an early red card and two goals led to the Kop chanting “Sacked in the morning” just 13 minutes into the Argentinian’s first game.

Chants of “Going down with the City” when the third goal went in – followed by “You’re not famous any more” and “Poch is at the wheel” – will only have made the trip back along the M62 more uncomfortable.

The match finished 4-0 when Victor Munoz slotted home in the 82nd minute, putting the seal on a disastrous bow in the United dugout for Pochettino.

"So painful, so disappointed,” Pochettino told Sky Sports. “It's not ok to start a game in the Premier League with this situation. The game changed completely after six minutes. Now we can explain everything but the damage is done, it's so painful.

"The players are so, so feeling the pain of the result. I told them to the calm: it was an unfair situation that happened. We need to accept that reality. We need to try to increase our focus, concentration and make better decisions on the field.

"We also need to be critical on ourselves but some situations happened in the game that we are not happy."

United’s all-time great boss Sir Alex Ferguson had a seat in the directors’ box alongside the actor and fan James Nesbitt – in Liverpool recording a new Poirot television show – and it was more a case of boiling blood than ‘Cold Feet’ at Anfield.

Ferguson had shared a pre-match joke with fellow Scot and long-time Liverpool rival Sir Kenny Dalglish about their choice of chocolate, but that was about as funny as it got for the 84-year-old.

There were also some stony faces from chief executive officer Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox, sat immediately in front of Ferguson, after a shambolic start for the new head coach.

#1029. Why was Leny Yoro sent off against Liverpool?

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Yoro was sent off inside eight minutes before Liverpool scored from the subsequent free-kick

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Life at Manchester United got off to a nightmare start for Mauricio Pochettino as his side was reduced to 10 men inside eight minutes in his managerial bow against Liverpool.

Liverpool started brightly and fashioned a chance out of nothing when Ronald Araujo’s hooked clearance left Matthijs de Ligt - making his first league start in a year - in no man’s land.

Alexander Isak latched onto the ball but was clattered into last man Leny Yoro just outside the box, prompting referee Sam Barrett to reach into his pocket and show the Frenchman a red card.

"It doesn't matter if you're playing with a back four, or back five, you've got to do the basics right. De Ligt - I'm amazed with him at this level,” Roy Keane said on Sky Sports.

"I know he's come back from an injury, he's just not reading the flight of the ball. If you do get it wrong, you run back, you sprint back, and then Yoro has got to be covering. If you're a defender, you always expect the worst."

There was a debate over whether VAR should have overturned the decision due to Isak’s heavy touch, which put into question he would have kept control of the ball - a key consideration in determining if a player has denied an obvious goalscoring opportunity (DOGSO).

"Isak's not getting the ball. There's no way he's getting the ball,” Keane added.

"It's clumsy from United. Obviously it's one straight ball over the top. You shouldn't be in so much trouble.

"But there's no way he's getting that ball. Absolutely not. I know Isak is quick and he's sharp, but we've looked at it again.

"It's really poor defending. Players not smelling danger. But Isak is not getting that ball. Absolutely not."

But VAR John Brooks did not call for a review, with the Premier League Match Centre writing in a statement: “The referee’s call of red card to Yoro for denial of an obvious goal-scoring opportunity (DOGSO) was checked and confirmed by VAR.

“REF: ‘It's a red card for DOGSO. On-field decision is outside [the box], red card, DOGSO’.

“VAR: ‘Defender bundles into him into the back, gets too tight, I think it's a foul’.”

Things then went from bad to worse for United as Dominik Szoboszlai stepped up to the free-kick and fired past Senne Lammens into the bottom-left corner, ensuring Yoro’s blunder was fully punished.

Liverpool doubled their lead just three minutes later, with Florian Wirtz volleying high into the goal as Pochettino’s side rapidly unravelled.

Liverpool’s outright domination of the opening stages, combined with losing a defender, sparked Pochettino into making an early change, replacing forward Bryan Mbeumo with centre-back Harry Maguire in the 22nd minute.

#1028. BMW reports lower Q3 earnings as China woes mount

BMW reports a drop in profits in the July to September quarter amid fierce competition from China.

German carmaker BMW reported a nearly 15% drop in third-quarter net profit on Wednesday, as competition from China shakes the global car industry.

Net profit for the third quarter fell to 1.45 billion euros ($1.61 billion), while sales fell nearly 6% to 30.45 billion euros, BMW said.

The main cause of the decline was BMW's poor business in China. Although the company sold more cars in the US and Europe compared to the same period last year, this could only partially offset the decline in China.

BMW's car deliveries in China, which were already at their lowest level since 2017 last year, fell 24.8% in the quarter and consequently dragged global deliveries down by 6.3.

CEO Milan Nedeljkovic said his company would "specifically intensify and accelerate structural measures."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

BMW on Tuesday also lowered its outlook for the current year, citing the faster-than-planned implementation of restructuring measures that includes 8,000 layoffs in its home market.

German carmakers have been struggling to compete with their Chinese counterparts in the electric vehicle market,  resulting in cost-cutting measures.

Volkswagen, the world's second-largest carmaker, is battling mounting competition from falling demand in its core Chinese market.

BMW, and its industry heavyweight peers, Volkswagen and Mercedes-Benz, have announced plans to scale back production and reduce costs.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Volkswagen Group posted its worst quarterly results in more than a decade earlier this October.

It is looking to cut about 15% of its workforce worldwide, or 100,000 jobs, by the end of the decade. BMW has announced that it will cut up to 8,000 jobs — about 5% of its workforce — by the end of 2027.

On the other hand, German auto parts supplier Schaeffler announced on Tuesday that it planned to cut almost 3,500 jobs and close five sites in Europe, by 2028.

According to the company statement, three-fourths of the 3,460 job cuts and four of the five site closures will be in Germany.

German automotive supplier Bosch, the world's biggest, announced last year that it would cut 13,000 jobs, mostly in its auto division.

The fiery Scot escaped a red card for his infamous tackle against Steaua Bucharest’s Marius Lacatus

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It’s fair to say that anyone would be spoilt for choice when it comes to selecting the most physical challenge of Graeme Souness’ career.

The fiery Scot was one of the most uncompromising players of his - or anyone else’s - generation, with the former Liverpool skipper taking no prisoners as he patrolled the middle of the park.

But even by his standards, one challenge stands out above all. That came in a European Cup tie against Steaua Bucharest in 1987, when Liverpool welcomed the Romanian side back to Anfield.

“We'd gone out there and lost the first leg 2-0,” Souness recalls to FourFourTwo. “There was a guy called Marius Lacatus who was going around topping people.

“In the second game, I thought, ‘If I get half a chance, I'll give him one.’”

It didn’t take long for that chance to present itself.

“After about 10 minutes, I went through this guy at groin height – when he went down and rolled over, I thought, ‘I've got the wrong player…' Lacatus was 15 or 20 yards away, laughing at me because he thought I was getting sent off.”

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Much to Souness’ surprise, that red card didn’t come.

“When I made the challenge, I thought, ‘F**k, I've got a problem here', so I went down as well, pretending someone had kicked me. It worked! I should have been arrested and spent time behind bars…”

The Scot would recieve his fair share of red and yellow cards during his illustrious playing career, but as he looks back on his career, he does not regret this approach.

“The reality is that I was sent off six or seven times in my career,” he continues. “Not bad given the nature of the game in those days. Every team had a couple of people who would get involved in the physical aspect.

“At Liverpool, people didn't say, ‘Oh we're playing Liverpool today, let's have a jolly nice game of football.' It was, ‘Let's put a few of them on their backsides and see how they deal with it.' If you stood up to that and it settled into a game of football, generally we'd win.

Graeme Souness' new book My Rangers is available now

For more than a decade, Joe Mewis has worked in football journalism as a reporter and editor. Mewis has had stints at Mirror Football and LeedsLive among others and worked at FourFourTwo throughout Euro 2024, reporting on the tournament. In addition to his journalist work, Mewis is also the author of four football history books that include times on Leeds United and the England national team. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

#1025. Why Manchester United will surpass Liverpool’s title drought

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation plus sign you up to our newsletter.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

The Red Devils are nearly halfway to matching their rivals’ 30-year title drought and there are no signs of it ending any time soon

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

“My greatest challenge was knocking Liverpool right off their f****** perch.”

Sir Alex Ferguson’s famous quote has become so embedded in football folklore that its provenance is often misremembered.

The then-Manchester United manager did not deliver the emphatic line in the early years of his tenure, as is sometimes claimed, but during a poor run of form in September 2002. The Red Devils had won seven of the previous 10 Premier League crowns, while Liverpool were not even halfway through their 30-year title drought.

Ferguson uttered that comment during Liverpool’s 13th successive campaign without winning the top flight. Fast forward almost a quarter of a century, and United are 13 years into a decline that set in as soon as the Scot retired.

The Red Devils’ title drought is already nearly half as long as the one Liverpool experienced between 1990 and 2020. They are in the Premier League relegation zone ahead of today’s trip to Anfield, so we can safely say their wait will stretch to at least the 2027/28 season, which will be 15 years since they last won the top flight.

Clearly, the 30-year mark is still a long way off and plenty can happen in that time. But it is also undeniable that United are as far from title challengers as they have been since 2013 and there are no signs of that changing.

That starts from the top. In September, executive co-chairman Avram Glazer told Deutsche Bank’s Sports Investment Conference in London that clubs of United’s stature are not dependent on success on the pitch for commercial power. The quotes, first reported by The Athletic, emerged this month when the Red Devils were about to sack manager Michael Carrick following their slide down the table.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Glazer’s comments were strikingly similar to those of former executive vice-chairman Ed Woodward in May 2018, when he told shareholders: “Playing performance doesn’t really have a meaningful impact on what we can do on the commercial side of the business.”

The fact that those two quotes occurred eight-and-a-half years apart suggests that as long as the Glazer family remain United’s majority owners, the club will prioritise commercial gain over on-pitch success.

The Americans also appear to be in no rush to sell their majority stake in the club, despite being universally unpopular with the fanbase. A report from TEAMtalk last week claimed they are unlikely to step away until United’s proposed 100,000-capacity stadium is built - which may not be until 2035 - in order to extract maximum value from their investment.

Other outlets claim the Glazers could be interested in selling their stake to co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe before then, but that certainly would not guarantee success, with the British businessman’s record in football across United, French club Nice and Swiss outfit Lausanne-Sport patchy at best.

When Ratcliffe bought a minority stake in the club in February 2024, taking control of sporting operations, it was supposed to end a decade of managerial mis-steps and overpaying for underperforming players.

However, the situation has deteriorated further, with chief executive officer Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox facing heavy criticism from fans. The Red Devils finished 15th in 2024/25 and have won just one league game this term, while the one positive half-season of the Ratcliffe era came when Carrick took over as interim boss from Ruben Amorim - another failed appointment - in January and overperformed expectations by qualifying for the Champions League.

Ultimately, United will not become a force again without an ownership change. As the Manchester United Supporters Trust (MUST) said in its statement following Carrick’s sacking: “Another change of head coach cannot repair what the ownership continues to undermine.”

This is where Liverpool’s title drought is instructive. Part of the reason for the Reds’ decline in the 1990s and 2000s was because they were overtaken financially by their rivals - initially Ferguson’s United, then Chelsea following Roman Abramovich’s takeover - under their long-time owners, the Moores family.

After the chaotic ownership of Tom Hicks and George Gillett, Fenway Sports Group (FSG) bought Liverpool in 2010. FSG did not get it right immediately, but after appointing Jurgen Klopp as manager in 2015 and putting the right people in key positions, such as sporting director Michael Edwards, the Reds were able to challenge regularly for the biggest honours again.

The team that won the title in 2020 featured some big-money recruits, most notably Virgil van Dijk and Alisson, but also several cheaper signings that resulted from a recruitment overhaul, such as Mo Salah, Roberto Firmino and Andy Robertson.

But the key point is that it took Liverpool 10 years of FSG ownership to end their title drought, and only once every department at the club, from the owners to the recruitment team to Klopp, were aligned in pursuit of on-pitch success.

It is why new United manager Mauricio Pochettino can only do so much. Like Carrick last season, Erik ten Hag in 2022/23 or Ole Gunnar Solskjaer in 2020/21, there may well be good spells during his tenure, but to paraphrase MUST, the head coach at Old Trafford will inevitably be undermined by the owners sooner or later.

Even when the Glazers eventually sell, we cannot expect the club to immediately become the force they once were, as the Liverpool example shows. It takes time to return to the top when you have been also-rans for so long.

That is why it is easy to see how United’s title drought could stretch beyond 30 years, as hypothetical as that sounds right now. If the Glazers stay in charge for the foreseeable future, the new owners would need time to undo the damage and put everything in place for success. Only then could United start to consistently challenge for the title and there is no guarantee they would win it straight away.

This scenario would have seemed unthinkable when Ferguson made his famous quip in 2002, but when you fall off your perch it is difficult to get back up - as Liverpool know all too well.

James Roberts is a freelance sports journalist working for FourFourTwo and other titles. He started his career at the Oxford Mail, where he covered Oxford United home and away, before becoming a sports sub-editor for various national newspapers.

#1024. Welcome to Man United, Mauricio Pochettino. It’s awful

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Liverpool 4-0 Manchester United: It took a 13-minute crash course for Pochettino to realise what he was in for as United were hammered by their rivals on his bow

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Welcome to Manchester United, Mauricio. For a man who had coveted the United job for years, this was an ignominious introduction. Mauricio Pochettino got a 13-minute crash course in the craziness of his new club. His first game was lost before he made his first substitution, and that came as early as the 22nd-minute. His debut brought the joint heaviest ever defeat by a United manager in his first game in charge, and the biggest in 100 years.

“So painful,” Pochettino said. “So disappointed.” As can be the way with United of late, most things that could go wrong did. When their new head coach’s name was sung, it was by the Kop. “Poch is at the wheel,” they taunted. A first meaningful day of work showed the scale of the task to steer United in the right direction.

The team who exhibited the pace and energy of the best Pochettino sides were Liverpool, relishing the chance to compound their rivals’ problems. Florian Wirtz scored a glorious goal, Bradley Barcola kept demonstrating a sprinter’s speed and Rio Ngumoha illuminated Anfield with his precocity. Yet each was aided by United, hapless and hopeless, showing it is easier to change the manager than to reverse one of the most extraordinary declines in English football history.

It was as though Pochettino’s charges had decided to show him a snapshot of the problems: their self-destructive streak, their defensive failings, their capacity to concede in quick succession. No previous Premier League manager had seen his side both let in two goals and go down to 10 men in the first half of his opening game. Pochettino’s United accomplished that in a quarter of an hour. Suffice to say there was no honeymoon period.

The watching Sir Alex Ferguson had lost his first game in charge, 2-0 at Oxford 40 years ago. Pochettino topped that, in the wrong way. Only Lal Hilditch, in 1926, had begun his reign as badly, with another 4-0 loss.

And yet there was a continuity to United’s calamity. Meet the new boss, same as the old boss? Despite regime change, some of this was very familiar. United were two goals behind after 18 minutes against Roma, after four against Villa, after 13 against Liverpool. United got rid of Michael Carrick, kept the masterplan of going 2-0 down and discovered it has certain flaws.

This was scarcely an unlucky 13 for United. Rather, they were culpable in their own downfall. Matthijs de Ligt needlessly left Ronald Araujo’s long ball, Alexander Isak ran behind the United defence and Leny Yoro barged him over. “It was an unfair situation,” complained Pochettino. “It was clear that was not a red card.” Iraola disagreed. “It is clearly the last man, clearly a foul,” he said.

So Yoro was sent off by referee Sam Barrott and waved off by the Liverpool faithful. The punishment for United was doubled when Dominik Szoboszlai drilled his free kick past a ramshackle wall and in. Chants of “going down” rang around Anfield. It was replaced, a few minutes later, by “sacked in the morning”.

With wonderful improvisation, Wirtz hooked in a volley after Ngumoha sped past Diogo Dalot and dinked in a cross. If a criticism was that the £100m German had influenced too few major matches in his Liverpool career, he altered this, brilliantly, and ended with an assist to accompany his second goal in as many games. “He's in a lovely moment,” said Iraola.

Liverpool slowed down at the end of the first half and then sped up again after the break. Barcola’s profligate finishing had cost him Liverpool’s third goal but his extraordinary pace created it. The £106m man’s scorched-earth solo run was followed by a pass to allow Ngumoha to replace Michael Owen as Liverpool’s youngest ever scorer against United. The teenager had tormented Dalot, but he was not the only winger on the scoresheet.

Victor Munoz exchanged passes with Wirtz and curled in the fourth after Liverpool’s high pressing was shown as Virgil van Dijk robbed Joshua Zirkzee, 25 yards from the United goal. Iraola ended doing fist pumps to the Kop, Jurgen Klopp-style.

“We probably should have scored more than four,” Iraola said. Senne Lammens saved, from Isak, Alexis Mac Allister and Szoboszlai. Harry Maguire made a brilliant block to turn an Isak shot away. The Swede slashed a shot wide after De Ligt inexplicably missed the ball for a second time.

It reflected badly on the new manager. Perhaps Pochettino’s first big call was to bring in De Ligt for a first league appearance of 2026. That backfired. Meanwhile, Maguire was first dropped and then summoned.

Pochettino had to keep changing tack. As Liverpool scored four goals, United used four formations. Pochettino seemed to begin by borrowing Ruben Amorim’s 3-4-3, then it looked a 4-2-3-1. Then it was neither, with United down to 10 men. “After what happened, happened and the plan was in the bin,” said Pochettino, who went to first 4-4-1 then 5-3-1, and who tried to argue what he felt was an injustice of a red card rendered what followed rather irrelevant. “We concede four goals with 10 men, and in a circumstance after playing 80 minutes at Anfield,” he said. But the circumstances are that United are in the relegation zone, lost on Pochettino’s bow, and were walloped by their rivals.

#1023. AI is ditching hallucinated references — and other bad habits

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Hallucinated academic citations have become a hallmark of the artificial-intelligence era. But they might soon be gone for good. Researchers have found that the latest large language models (LLMs) rarely, if ever, attribute information to sources that don’t exist.

The finding is part of an analysis that reports that many LLM tendencies, such as overthinking simple mathematics problems and complying with illogical requests, fade over time as AI companies release new or updated models with improved capabilities. Many of these tendencies disappear about 16 months after the phenomenon is first described in a published paper. The analysis, described in a blogpost, has not been peer reviewed.

“We, as users of these systems, need to not have such a fixed view of what AI can do and what it can’t do,” says co-author Owen Queen, an AI researcher at Stanford University in California.

But just because an LLM behaviour fades as models improve doesn’t mean that the effect immediately disappears, says Maxim Topaz, a health-care AI researcher at Columbia University in New York City. Topaz has found1 that the number of hallucinated citations in academic papers has risen drastically since 2023, probably because more researchers than ever before are using LLMs, and they often aren’t using the latest models.

Queen and his colleague identified 50 widely cited LLM behaviours that were described in publications between late 2022, when some of the first LLMs became widely available, and late 2025. They then gave the same prompts that first elicited the behaviour in the original publications to 20 LLMs that were released from mid-2024 to late 2026 to see if the effect has strengthened or weakened over time. For example, they asked each model to count the number of r’s in ‘strawberry’ — something that LLMs have found difficult but can now do more reliably.

Nearly half of the behaviours they checked have largely disappeared from newer models, leading the researchers to deem those effects ‘expired’. Expired behaviours had an average lifespan of about 16 months after publication, although some were fleeting — models stopped overthinking simple maths problems just a month and a half after this tendency was published. Other traits persisted, such as the stereotyping of Black women by disproportionately describing them as resilient, which lasted for longer than three years.

Although most of the retested LLM behaviours have faded over time, three have become more pronounced. Today’s models praise what their users like even more often than they used to, LLMs favour their own writing more strongly than that of other LLMs and people; and LLMs are now even worse than they used to be at generating truly random numbers.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03753-1

Topaz, M., Roguin, N., Gupta, P., Zhanga, Z. & Peltonen, L.-M. Lancet 407, 1779–1781 (2026).

Article  PubMed  Google Scholar

Walters, W. H. & Wilder, E. I. Sci. Rep. 13, 14045 (2023).

#1021. Mauricio Pochettino fumes over red card decision after nightmare start to life at Manchester United

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Pochettino and Kobbie Mainoo both denied that Leny Yoro should have been sent off for a last-man challenge on Alexander Isak

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

New Manchester United manager Mauricio Pochettino has denied that Leny Yoro should have been sent off in his side’s 4-0 loss to Liverpool, calling it an “unfair situation”.

Yoro was given a straight red card in the eighth minute of the game at Anfield to give Pochettino the worst possible start to his life as United boss, with the young Frenchman fouling the Liverpool striker after he had gone clean through as last man.

As there was no attempt to play the ball, referee Sam Barrott showed Yoro a straight red card, with VAR checking and confirming the decision “for denial of an obvious goal-scoring opportunity (DOGSO)”.

It went from bad to worse for United too, with Dominik Szoboszlai scoring from 19 yards out from the ensuing free-kick.

But while little was made of the incident at the time, some – including Roy Keane in the Sky Sports studio – pointed out that the challenge may not have been worthy of a red card as Isak was unlikely to stay in control of the ball after taking a poor touch.

And Pochettino agreed, stating that “the ball was for the goalkeeper”.

“In that situation, if you review the VAR you can see for sure, he [Yoro] never had the intention to connect with Isak,” explained Pochettino on Sky Sports after full-time.

“When the control was long with the striker, the ball was going to the goalkeeper, he runs and goes down. In Leny's case, it wasn't intentional. It was an unusual situation that is normal, everyone who plays football can feel it.

"We have to take responsibility, I take the responsibility. We keep pushing. It's not going to change what happened. Being respectful is the most important. At the same time, I have to defend my club. And tell what I feel. That was an action that everyone who plays football, it was clear that a situation that was not a red card,” he added.

Kobbie Mainoo agreed with his manager, saying there is “no chance” it deserved to be a sending off.

“The ball's already with the goalkeeper. They're both running full speed. What can we do? It is what it is,” said the United midfielder.

The result leaves United in 19th after 11 games, with just eight points and one win in the league all season. As for Liverpool, they rise to fourth with 21 points, just seven behind leaders Arsenal.

#1020. Leading ice hockey nations, sponsors oppose Russia's return

Ice hockey's governing body says the impact of a court decision forcing it to reinstate Russia presents "significant practical and sporting challenges." Several leading nations say they won't play against Russian teams.

The International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) said in a statement on Wednesday that the impact of last week's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) decision requiring it to reinstate Russia to international play had been "significantly underestimated."

It added that it "maintains" its disagreement with the decision and that it remained "in dialogue with Member National Associations, organizing committees, host authorities and other key stakeholders to determine the best way forward."

Shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the IIHF barred its teams from competing in international ice hockey tournaments, citing security concerns. In last Friday's ruling, the CAS said that the IIHF's concerns were "not supported by sufficient evidence."

Wednesday's statement comes after two days of talks by the IIHF Council aimed at charting a way forward following Friday's CAS decision, which appears to have caught most of the international ice hockey community off guard.

Two of the organizing committees the statement refers to are those of Canada, which is due to host the IIHF World Junior Championship starting next month, and Germany, which is to host the IIHF Men's World Championship next May. Both countries are strong supporters of Ukraine in its war against Russia, and both have expressed serious reservations about their upcoming tournaments in light of the CAS ruling.

On Tuesday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney ruled out allowing Russians to compete in the World Juniors in Alberta.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," he told reporters at a press conference in Antigua, where he was attending a Commonwealth meeting.

"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there."

Last weekend, Frank Lutz, chairman of the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) conceded in a television interview that following the CAS decision, the DEB would "also have to consider the option of handing back (hosting rights to) this championship."

In a statement to DW on Wednesday, a German government spokesperson reiterated Berlin's position on the matter from the weekend, saying it viewed Friday's CAS ruling "very critically."

The spokesperson also said  the government would "consult with the German Ice Hockey Federation in the near future regarding the potential consequences of this decision, including its impact on the 2027 Ice Hockey World Championship in Germany."

Meanwhile, the ice hockey association of Finland, the defending men's world champions, has been spearheading an effort to boycott upcoming IIHF tournaments should the Russians be allowed to compete.

"We are currently working to bring as many countries as possible into a united front to tell the IIHF that none of us will play against Russia under these circumstances," Finnish Ice Hockey Association boss Heikki Hietanen said in a statement released on the organization's website on Monday.

"Our stance is that we will not play against Russia as long as the war of aggression against Ukraine continues," added Hietanen, who is also a member of the IIHF Council.

Sweden, Norway, Denmark and Czechia have since made similar statements.

"The Three Crowns will not play Russia in coming world championship tournaments," Swedish Ice Hockey Federation boss Anders Larsson said.

This came shortly after Norway said it would not play Russia at the Men's World Championship and the Danish Ice Hockey Federation issued a similar statement on its website.

"Denmark will – based on the current situation and the information available to us today – not play against Russia at the World Championship in Germany in May 2027," it read. Denmark did not qualify for the World Juniors.

Czechia Ice Hockey Association President Alois Hadamczik confirmed on Tuesday that they too would refrain from playing Russian teams.

Latvia's federation said it “reaffirms its longstanding and firm position" not to play against Russia or its ally Belarus.

Alexander Helwig, chairman of the Austrian Ice Hockey Association told public broadcaster ORF that “as of now, we would certainly not play against Russia."

USA Hockey has yet to comment on the CAS ruling.

At the same time, sponsors of IIHF tournaments are also getting cold feet. Skoda, which has been the main sponsor of the Men's World Championship for more than three decades, told the Associated Press that it would "reassess" its position if Russia takes part.

"We do not support the Court of Arbitration for Sport's decision regarding the participation of Russian national teams in IIHF competitions. With Russia's aggression continuing, we believe the Russian national team's return to the world championship is incompatible with the values we have consistently upheld," the Czech carmaker said.

Skoda isn't alone either, Finnish tire manufacturer Nokian had said it would end its backing if Russia took part and Swedish furniture maker AJ Products, whose logo has been seen on the boards and officials' jerseys at World Championships since 1989, said Monday it would ask for its logo not to be shown.

On Wednesday afternoon, yet another sponsor joined the list, with German workwear company Strauss saying it would "forgo all logo exposure associated with the (men's) tournament" and was considering withdrawing its sponsporship entirely.

With the IIHF Council having failed to agree on how to proceed during its meetings on Monday and Tuesday, President Franz Reindl told Germany's SID news agency on Wednesday, that it would reconvene for further talks on Thursday.

This article was originally published on November 4, 2026. It was updated on November 5, 2026 with the German government statement to DW.

SEE ALSO Interactive football calendar 2026/27: Every game in every competition

It means this is Blackburn's best chance in a long time of beating their rivals, having gone 11 games without a victory in this fixture since a 1-0 win at Turf Moor in the Premier League in 2010.

However, it would be understandable if their minds are elsewhere after manager Tony Mowbray stepped back from his role due to health issues this week. Assistant head coaches Damien Johnson and Mike Dodds are in joint caretaker charge in his absence.

The 62-year-old is hugely popular within the game and had steered Blackburn to 13th in the table before the international break — a welcome change after last season's relegation battle.

Rovers will be without goalkeeper Balazs Toth after he suffered an injury on international duty with Hungary, which will see Aynsley Pears step in. Sam Morsy, Scott Wharton and Andri Gudjohnsen are doubtful, while Mathias Jorgensen is sidelined, but Ryoya Morishita looks set to return to the squad.

The Clarets are really struggling and Rovers could take advantage to claim a famous win.

Liverpool 4-0 Manchester United: Pochettino’s nightmares come true as 10-man United were outclassed by their north-west rivals

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Mauricio Pochettino endured the worst possible start to life as Manchester United manager as his side were thrashed 4-0 by fierce rivals Liverpool.

United set the tone for a disastrous afternoon early as they went a man down inside eight minutes, with Leny Yoro bundling into Alexander Isak as the last man to be shown a straight red card.

Dominik Szoboszlai fired in from the resulting free-kick to ensure Yoro’s blunder was fully punished, and Liverpool doubled their lead three minutes later when Florian Wirtz excellently improvised a volley to score.

Rio Ngumoha got a deserved goal after the break to put the game to bed, converting from Bradley Barcola’s cross, before Victor Munoz put the cherry on a ruthless performance for the hosts late on.

Follow updates from Liverpool v Man United, below:

Welcome to Manchester United, Mauricio. For a man who had coveted the United job for years, this was an ignominious introduction. Mauricio Pochettino got a 13-minute crash course in the craziness of his new club. His first game was lost before he made his first substitution, and that came as early as the 22nd-minute. His debut brought the joint heaviest ever defeat by a United manager in his first game in charge, and the biggest in 100 years.

“So painful,” Pochettino said. “So disappointed.” As can be the way with United of late, most things that could go wrong did. When their new head coach’s name was sung, it was by the Kop. “Poch is at the wheel,” they taunted. A first meaningful day of work showed the scale of the task to steer United in the right direction.

Mauricio Pochettino endured a dismal start to his tenure at Manchester United as Liverpool ran riot in a 4-0 victory against their relegation-threatened rivals.

A whirlwind week for the former Argentina international ended in familiar disappointment for the struggling visitors, whose hopes of a new manager bounce were decisively crushed during a nightmare opening 13 minutes at Anfield.

Dominik Szoboszlai put the hosts ahead with a fierce free-kick after defender Leny Yoro was sent off for denying a goalscoring opportunity inside just eight minutes, before Florian Wirtz’s smart finish quickly put Pochettino’s side further behind.

By the end, amid what Xabi Alonso described as a “fragile moment”, even his own cultured touch had deserted him. As his Chelsea team tried to offer something in the final minutes of an utterly nothing performance against a brilliant Leeds United, the ball was easily cleared for a throw. Alonso, famed for his technique as a player, miscontrolled it towards his underwhelming bench.

He’s now seeing his reputation as a coach plummet, as Chelsea fall to eighth. This 4-1 evisceration was not just Leeds’ first win at the home of their old Seventies rivals since 1999 – to add to how Tottenham Hotspur also won here a few weeks ago – but a second defeat in a row, and a fifth in 11 this season.

And yet the very nature of it was still worse than any numbers can tell.

i Madueke snatched a 2-2 draw for Arsenal after Newcastle produced a stunning second-half turnaround to claim a deserved point against the Premier League leaders.

Eberechi Eze put the champions in front and Madueke wasted a couple of chances to increase the lead before half-time, with Matthias Jaissle’s side jeered off following a listless first 45 minutes.

They rallied in stunning fashion on the resumption, with Harvey Barnes scoring Newcastle’s first goal at St James’ Park since September 19 before Malick Thiaw put them ahead after the hour from close range.

The best part of five hours after the final whistle blew at the Etihad Stadium and about 150 miles north east, Noni Madueke scored an equaliser to ensure the day ended with the equation ultimately unchanged. Manchester City will still go to Arsenal on Sunday six points behind the reigning champions. They could reduce the gap to three, though the evidence of recent weeks is that it is likelier to stretch to nine.

That would surely end City’s title challenge. The theory had been that it would take a potential punishment for their 114 guilty verdicts to do that and, while City are appealing, a sizeable sanction may be still to come. Perhaps that is fitting: the title could be decided on the pitch, rather than in the courts.

Mauricio Pochettino is the manager Manchester United could, time and again, have appointed in the past. He marked his eventual arrival at Old Trafford by trying to shrug it off; theirs more than his. Pochettino made it to the last two in 2022, when Erik ten Hag was instead chosen, and may have seemed United’s second choice in 2016 and 2019, when Jose Mourinho and Ole Gunnar Solskjaer were preferred. But by pivoting to the future was a way of avoiding the issue of why none of them – nor David Moyes, Louis van Gaal, Ralf Rangnick, Ruben Amorim or Michael Carrick – has truly succeeded.

Pochettino’s plan to fix United may draw on a more distant past, the identity he described that seemed to stem more from Sir Alex Ferguson than his eight immediate successors, but reliant heavily on a positivity about the future. “I don't think too much in the past. I think if we want to create something different and positive and the people feel proud about that, it’s to build our own way.”

Life at Manchester United got off to a nightmare start for Mauricio Pochettino as his side was reduced to 10 men inside eight minutes in his managerial bow against Liverpool.

Liverpool started brightly and fashioned a chance out of nothing when Ronald Araujo’s hooked clearance left Matthijs de Ligt - making his first league start in a year - in no man’s land.

#1016. How Man United fans revolted against the Glazers to create their own football club

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation plus sign you up to our newsletter.

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Play the viral 442GOALS game and build an XI of Premier League legends!

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Fantastic football content straight to your inbox! From the latest transfer news, quizzes, videos, features and interviews with the biggest names in the game, plus lots more.

Sign up to our FREE live football newsletter, tracking all of the biggest games available to watch on the device of your choice. Never miss a kick-off!

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

Horrified at the Glazer family’s impending takeover two decades ago, a group of Manchester United fans went to church. FC United was their divine inspiration, a phoenix club born at the heart of the community

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Revolution can spark in the most unlikely places. John Lennon knew that. The former Beatle and wife Yoko Ono needed only an Amsterdam hotel room to stage their 1969 protest over the Vietnam War. Lennon’s decision to start a revolution from his bed would later be immortalised in the lyrics of Oasis’ Imagine pastiche Don’t Look Back in Anger.

Fully 36 years after that legendary ‘bed-in’, a group of football supporters chose an equally unlikely venue to kick-start their own revolution. Outraged by a hostile takeover of their beloved Manchester United, and fed up with where football appeared to be heading in general, they convened in May 2005 to discuss a notion that would send shockwaves through the English game. The meeting place: Methodist Central Hall in Manchester’s Northern Quarter.

“There was a buzz in the air,” explains Jules Spencer, a lifelong Manchester United fan who attended the event and had taken part in other protests. “We’d fought against change before, including Rupert Murdoch’s attempted takeover. But this was the final straw.”

Back in 1999, the United Kingdom’s Competition Commission had blocked Murdoch and BSkyB’s £625 million bid for Manchester United, the government’s reasoning that the acquisition would have “hurt competition in the broadcast industry and the quality of British football”. The next major power grab would not be so easily thwarted, though.

Malcolm Glazer, an American business tycoon and owner of NFL franchise the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, had first bought nearly three per cent of Manchester United in March 2003. Through a series of incremental buyouts, that stake neared 30 per cent by October 2004 – a threshold above which Glazer would have to launch a formal takeover bid.

Businessmen muscling into football was nothing new, but as the takeover drew nearer supporters became increasingly concerned. Most of the capital used by Glazer to buy the club would come in the form of loans, the majority of which were secured against the club’s assets, incurring average interest payments of more than £46m per annum.

“It was,” lifelong Red Devils fan Paul Hurst says, “absolutely scandalous.”

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

In February 2005, hundreds of United fans protested outside Old Trafford, with some hanging an effigy of Glazer. That month, the idea for a breakaway club was first mooted by now defunct fanzine Red Issue.

“As the spectre of Malcolm Glazer looms ever larger, the question has been increasingly asked: ‘What would you do if he did take over?’” they penned. “What if you could give up supporting Glazer’s company without giving up United?

“Back in the days of the Murdoch campaign, an evacuation plan was drawn up, detailing the blueprint for the formation of a new Manchester United, one which spurned the commercialism and tackiness of the modern game, and was controlled and run by the fans. With United again under threat, those plans have been resurrected. With a working name of ‘FC United’, the logistics of the operation to set up a new Manchester United has been looked into.”

The article outlined the bold ambition. “We would await regime change, while aiding all attempts to undermine the illegitimate occupation,” it continued. “When Glazer is defeated, FC United will be happy to return to Old Trafford and merge with ‘the franchise’ on condition that the supporters’ trust maintains full ownership of the football club and the unified Manchester United take over the higher league position of FC United. Viva la revolucion.”

Three months later, Glazer completed his takeover, reaching the 75 per cent threshold required to end the club’s public limited company (PLC) status and delist from the London Stock Exchange.

It prompted fans to assemble and discuss a new club at Methodist Central Hall, complete with Styrofoam cups of tea in hand, surrounded by murals of Bible scenes and psalms.

“I’d taken part in the protests against the Glazers, along with so many others,” says Hurst, who was at that meeting. “Many of us pledged not to give the club one penny more while Glazer owned it. We wouldn’t be paying off his debts.”

“It wasn’t about switching off our allegiance to Manchester United – that would never go,” remembers Spencer. “It was about letting Manchester United and the Glazers know that we wouldn’t stand idly by and allow this to happen. If necessary, we were willing to put our money towards something else instead, something positive to be proud of.”

Red Issue editor John-Paul O’Neill organised the new movement, backed by a steering committee. “It was drawn from across the fanbase, from official fan groups to business people and those with marketing and communications expertise,” says team member Spencer. “We held more meetings, with around 1,500 people joining at Manchester’s Apollo theatre. Not everybody was convinced, but they came along to hear what we had to say. Momentum began to build and some fans started to pledge their United season ticket money to help us get off the ground. It was so exciting.”

Preparations included a visit from Kris Stewart, chairman of AFC Wimbledon, founded three years earlier. “His insight was invaluable,” recalls Spencer. “We didn’t really know what we were doing at that stage. He told us we were in for a lot of hard work and that a lot would go wrong, but it’d be totally worth it if we pulled it off. He remained a valued sounding board in the months to come.”

Time was of the essence. The new club had to be set up and registered well before the new 2005-06 season, already less than two months away. Failing to do so would risk losing momentum. They didn’t even have a name.

The FA vetoed ‘FC United’ for being too generic, so those who’d pledged money were asked to vote on a different name. Manchester Central and Newton Heath United were discarded as options – in June, ‘FC United of Manchester’ got the nod and joined the 10th-tier North West Counties Division Two. While it wasn’t their official moniker, many called them FC United anyway

There was still the not insignificant issue of finding some players. Some 900 applications were whittled down to 200 trialists, from which Karl Marginson, the club’s inaugural manager, would select a squad of 17.

“The standard of the trialists was very strong and we put together a team I felt capable of challenging for the title in our first campaign,” he tells FFT now.

How did the manager get the gig? “It was between me and one other bloke, and he was a Scouser,” Marginson, a born-and-bred Manc chuckles. “I was 34 – I’d been an assistant at Flixton, so not had a proper manager’s job before, but I knew the league well.

“I’d been a Manchester United fan all my life and didn’t like where the original club was heading. I didn’t think my own kids would be able to afford to go when they were old enough, the way I had as a teenager, and that was so wrong. The new club was important and I think they could see what it meant to me as well. I was young and ambitious – the idea of taking charge of a totally new club appealed to me.”

Their first match was a drab 0-0 draw at Leigh RMI. The pre-season friendly was watched by more than 2,500 fans, TV crews and national journalists. “It was magnificent and bonkers at the same time,” says Marginson. “There was a party atmosphere in the air, even for such a terrible game. I couldn’t believe what I’d let myself in for.”

A similar-sized crowd flocked to FC United’s first competitive match, a 5-2 victory at Leek County School Old Boys, whose ground was used to hosting fans by the dozen, not the thousand. Home matches, staged at Bury’s Gigg Lane as part of a long-term groundsharing deal, delivered gates as large as 6,000 during a season that consistently smashed the league’s attendance records.

“It was incredible to see,” reminisces future board member Hurst. “The level of football was very different to what we’d been used to, nine divisions higher in the Premier League, but the sense of community more than made up for it.”

The matchday mood wasn’t always positive, though. Throughout the club’s formation, a small yet vocal group of Manchester United supporters had railed against the movement, branding those involved traitors. Tensions flared during a game against Salford City. “The fixture had to be switched to Salford’s rugby league ground due to the expected crowd,” explains Hurst.

“Lots of Manchester United fans bought tickets to protest against us, which was ironic. They had some banners calling us turncoats and all the rest of it. It got quite unpleasant.”

Even Sir Alex Ferguson weighed in on the new club, labelling the movement “a shame” and questioning whether those involved were really proper Red Devils to begin with.

“Listen, we could all understand the criticism to a certain degree,” continues Hurst. “The new club was divisive, even within families and friendship circles.

“There were those that saw it as the genuine protest movement it was – a necessary act of defiance – and others who saw us as Judases who turned our back on the club in its hour of need. That was never the case.

“Many of us are passionate Manchester United supporters. We just didn’t want to fund Glazer’s debts by going to games. Thankfully, a lot of that hatred has died down since.”

On-field headlines were positive. The Red Rebels swept to the Division Two title in their first season, finishing eight points clear of Marginson’s former club Flixton. “A fantastic achievement,” he says. “It was important to show that we were a club that meant business in footballing terms as well, beyond the protest club element.”

They were far from done. FC United won promotion again in their second campaign, then another in their third to reach the Northern Premier Division, two levels below the National League and three from the EFL.

A fourth promotion was squandered in 2010-11, courtesy of a play-off final defeat to Colwyn Bay. Earlier in that season, FC United had advanced to the FA Cup first round for the first time, then won at League One Rochdale to set up a second round showdown at Brighton, who would go on to win the third tier that term.

The 10-man Red Rebels even led at the Withdean Stadium, before Mauricio Taricco’s late equaliser earned Gus Poyet’s Seagulls a replay they would win 4-0 at Gigg Lane. The 6,900 gate that night was more than 1,500 higher than the first encounter in East Sussex.

Further play-off defeats followed in 2012, 2013 and 2014. “I definitely felt the pressure to win matches and keep taking the football club forward,” says Marginson. “I was still inexperienced and we were getting huge attendances to every game.

“We had one of the bigger budgets in those leagues and supporters expected a lot. I already drank alcohol, but I’d be lying if I said I didn’t lean into that a bit more to help cope.”

Promotion eventually came in 2015 – not only did FC United secure a fifth successive top-six finish, this time they won the league, during a campaign in which they groundshared with Curzon Ashton and Stalybridge Celtic. “It was an epic achievement,” says Marginson with pride. “The club stuck by me and we got there in the end.”

The timing couldn’t have been better, with a new 4,700-capacity home all of their own ready to move into.

“Gigg Lane served us incredibly well, but financially it made more sense for us to have somewhere permanent,” says director Hurst. “We scouted out a number of sites before the council let us build a new stadium in Moston.”

Located just four miles north-east of Manchester city centre, Broadhurst Park cost £6.5m and hosted its first match, a friendly against Benfica B, on May 29 that year – the same date on which Manchester United beat Benfica in the 1968 European Cup Final. “It felt like a massive step for us,” adds Spencer. “A place to stand with our friends, our sons and daughters, and call home.”

FC United finished a respectable 13th in the National League North on two occasions, but a tough start to 2017-18 resulted in Marginson’s exit. “If you’d have told me when I first took the job that I’d still have been there all those years later, I’d have said, ‘No chance’,” he says, reflecting on 12 years in charge. “I think back to the young man I was when I became manager – it’s a world apart. I couldn’t have done the job had I been older. It needed youth and energy from the off. Eventually, I ran out.”

A new injection arrived in the form of striker Tom Greaves – the club’s all-time top scorer – who stepped up to a player-manager role. He steered the club to survival but departed after a poor start to the next campaign, to be replaced by Neil Reynolds. He, though, couldn’t turn the tide, with FC United relegated back to the Northern Premier Division. COVID annulled 2019-20 when they were sat second and set for the play-offs again – five years on, they’re yet to return to the sixth tier of the pyramid.

Not that it’s all been doom and gloom. Later in 2020, FC United reached the FA Cup first round for the third time, facing League One Doncaster Rovers in front of the live TV cameras. A year after that, they were invited to participate in the inaugural Fenix Trophy, a tournament contested by a selection of unusual non-league sides from across Europe. The Mancunians travelled to face AKS Zly in Warsaw, and Brera in Milan, going on to beat Prague Raptors in the final in the Italian city of Rimini.

In 2022-23, they again reached the latter stages of the competition, losing a semi to BK Skjold of Denmark but then beating Brera at Milan’s San Siro, no less. Last season, after matches in Krakow and Paris, they won the cup for a second time, defeating Prague Raptors in the final once more, on the shores of Lake Garda on this occasion.

“I certainly didn’t envisage leading my team-mates out at San Siro when I first joined,” says club captain Charlie Ennis, who arrived in the summer of 2019. “Getting changed in Milan’s dressing room and walking out onto that iconic pitch – it still gives me goosebumps now. We’ve been very lucky to be a part of the competition, travelling across Europe. It’s been one of the highlights of my career.”

Ennis, now 34, is another who didn’t expect to stay as long as he has. “I was no spring chicken when I signed,” he jokes. “But I’m a local lad and, short of playing for Manchester United, who I grew up supporting, there’s nowhere else I’d rather be. We get big crowds, play at a fantastic ground and this club means so much to people. The best years are yet to come.”

The man tasked with leading them into the next era is gaffer Mark Beesley, who replaced Reynolds in September after resigning from Warrington Town. His squad includes 38-year-old former Reading and Bolton forward Adam Le Fondre, a lifelong Manchester United fan who spoke of semi-fulfilling a dream when signing from Scottish Premiership side Hibernian last summer.

Whatever the future holds, FC United can already look back on the past two decades with enormous pride. “It’s been a lot of hard work, but I wouldn’t have changed it for the world,” director Hurst tells FFT now. “You look over at Manchester United, what continues to happen at the club with its ownership, and you’d be hard pressed to say we were wrong to do this. We’ve given local football fans a positive alternative.”

Manchester United are still majority-owned by the Glazers. Malcolm passed the reins to his sons before his death in 2014. Since the family took charge, it’s estimated the club has paid out more than £750m in interest fees on loan repayments alone. Debts remain high, while on-field success has steadily declined since Ferguson’s retirement. Ineos impresario Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s £1bn investment for a 27.7 per cent stake has rekindled neither success nor spirit.

“We want more than anything for that to change, for the Glazers to sell up, and for Manchester United to become a well-run club again,” says Spencer. “I’m still a Manchester United fan. I was jumping for joy when we beat City in last season’s FA Cup final. But as long as the Glazers are still there, I can’t be.”

Until that day, and long after, Spencer and his fellow rebels will be found at Broadhurst Park. “I come here with my sons and it’s a special feeling,” he says. “It’s something positive that we can all share as a community. I look back at that meeting at the church hall all those years ago and can’t help but laugh at how far we’ve come since. We made the right decision.

Ed is a staff writer at FourFourTwo, working across the magazine and website. A German speaker, he’s been working as a football reporter in Berlin since 2015, predominantly covering the Bundesliga and Germany's national team. Favourite FFT features include an exclusive interview with Jude Bellingham following the youngster’s move to Borussia Dortmund in 2020, a history of the Berlin Derby since the fall of the Wall and a celebration of Kevin Keegan’s playing career.

#1015. Liverpool vs Man United player ratings: Two 9/10s inspire as Mauricio Pochettino endures nightmare bow

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Liverpool 4-0 Manchester United: Rio Ngumoha and Florian Wirtz starred as Mauricio Pochettino endured horror in his first game as United manager

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Mauricio Pochettino endured a dismal start to his tenure at Manchester United as Liverpool ran riot in a 4-0 victory against their relegation-threatened rivals.

A whirlwind week for the former Argentina international ended in familiar disappointment for the struggling visitors, whose hopes of a new manager bounce were decisively crushed during a nightmare opening 13 minutes at Anfield.

Dominik Szoboszlai put the hosts ahead with a fierce free-kick after defender Leny Yoro was sent off for denying a goalscoring opportunity inside just eight minutes, before Florian Wirtz’s smart finish quickly put Pochettino’s side further behind.

United managed to temporarily stem the tide courtesy of crucial Senne Lammens saves, last-ditch defending, and wayward finishing, but Andoni Iraola’s side redoubled their efforts after the interval.

Pochettino’s 10 men were frankly fortunate that Liverpool only added two more goals through Rio Ngumoha and substitute Victor Munoz, such was the overwhelming nature of their dominance.

Here are how the players rated at Anfield:

Smart stop to deny Fernandes when Man United started knocking at the door in the first half, alive to the situation after not being required in the early stages. Barely got a touch after the break, until being called until action in stoppage time to deny Fernandes consolation.

His through ball for Isak was more of a hooked clearance than a calculated lofted pass, but it still caused the chaos required to get Yoro sent off. Always willing to get in the challenge. Subbed.

Defensively sound and looked comfortable enough to sometimes step into midfield, especially when United were forced into removing an attacker to sure up their defence. Smart play to deal with a Fernandes run in behind during the second half, using his pace to get goalside and draw the foul.

Dominated physically with United not having a recognised striker on the pitch. Was similarly comfortable against the challenge of Zirkzee.

Shaky to start against Mbeumo, fortunate the Cameroonian was the sacrifice after Yoro’s red.

Superbly fired home from the free-kick to fully punish the Yoro blunder and always Liverpool’s engine room. Had a fair few pops from range that got Lammens scrambling.

Liverpool’s metronome and came up with some delightful passes as the hosts had fun at United’s expense. Subbed.

Full of running and pace but struggled to figure out when to pull the trigger, which wasted the opportunities he forged himself. The third chance he missed was a real sitter - and he made an absolute mess of it. Made up for earlier misses with a nice assist for Ngumoha. Subbed.

Excellent volley to double Liverpool’s lead and thrived in the space created by Liverpool’s man advantage, bringing his fine international form back to his club. Signed off on a brilliant performance with a delightful assist for Munoz.

A real demon on the left, terrorising Dalot and often leaving the Portuguese defender in his dust. Excellent work to assist Wirtz and got his deserved goal to put the game to bed, becoming this fixture’s youngest scorer in Premier League history. Some talent. Subbed.

Really impressive on the whole, with the only thing missing being the goal. Looking sharp, he drew the foul that got Yoro sent off and was a constant threat against United, forcing Lammens into multiple saves before the break. He should have found the net after the break as he beared down on goal after another De Ligt error, but wildly blazed wide. Still deserves his flowers. Subbed.

Victor Munoz (Barcola, 72’) - 8: Did what Barcola couldn’t on this glorious afternoon for Liverpool and gobbled up the chance that fell to him. Good finish.

Trey Nyoni (Mac Allister, 72’) - 7: Solid cameo from the highly-rated midfielder, who got a warm welcome when he came on.

Jeremie Frimpong (Ngumoha, 78’) - 6: Susceptible to the odd error but too late for any damage to be done or anyone to care. Ran for a bit.

Joe Gomez (Araujo, 85’) - N/A: Still no goal.

Beaten on the goalkeeper’s side for Szoboszlai’s free-kick, which wasn’t a good look. However, he couldn’t do a huge amount for Wirtz and Ngumoha’s goals, and he made a fair few saves to limit the scoreline and technically keep United in the game for a while. It could’ve been seven again.

Sent off inside eight minutes. Debate over whether Isak had control of the ball but no excuse for bundling into him like that. Put his side at an instant disadvantage.

First start in a year and he looked completely out of his depth. No man’s land for Araujo’s hook that led to Yoro’s red and was very nearly guilty. Subbed.

United’s best starting defender but that’s not exactly high praise. Put in a flying challenge to deny Barcola a goal in the second half.

Really struggled against the pace and skill of Ngumoha, losing nearly every duel with the electrifying teenager. Not much to offer going forward.

Inconsistent in possession and often far too passive, at one point just passing it straight to Mac Allister to spark a Liverpool counter attack, from which they nearly scored. Subbed.

Similarly struggled in the double pivot as Liverpool’s man advantage saw United get overrun, but had a couple flashes of brilliance - like when he tried to set Bruno Fernandes away in the second half from his defensive final third with a superb threaded pass. Subbed.

Started brightly against Kerkez but was the sacrifice when United needed another defender. Subbed early.

The only one to really test Alisson throughout, forcing the Brazilian into a smart save in the first half before nearly netting a consolation in stoppage time. Nevertheless uninspiring and lost a lot of his battles in the middle of the park.

Physically struggled against Van Dijk and Jacquet, and subbed at half-time by a natural No 9 who could maybe handle that sort of challenge.

Harry Maguire (Mbeumo, 22’) - 6: United gained a semblance of control after his arrival, something they kept hold of until half-time. But things fell apart again after half-time - couldn’t keep up with Ngumoha for Liverpool’s third.

Joshua Zirkzee (Cunha, 46’) - 5: Brought on to give United some sort of presence up top and went unnoticed. Gave the ball away for Liverpool’s fourth.

Noussair Mazraoui (Dorgu, 65’) - 5: Not exactly the game-changer United needed at this moment, and they conceded two minutes after his arrival.

Mason Mount (Tielemans, 65’) - 6: Not much to offer with Liverpool dominating the ball.

Andrey Santos (Mainoo, 87’) - N/A: Minutes.

The Celtic great moved south of the border in 1977

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When Kenny Dalglish arrived at Liverpool from Celtic in 1977, he arrived as a 26-year-old, just entering his peak years.

Signed as a replacement for Hamburg-bound Kop icon Kevin Keegan, Dalglish eclipsed even King Kev’s achievements in Reds shirt over the next decade and a half.

But the Scot’s move to Anfield almost happened a decade earlier, when he was still a teenager.

“Myself and another boy were invited for trials with Liverpool when I was a teenager,” Dalglish tells FourFourTwo. “We played a game, then I was asked to go back for a couple of weeks.

“Shanks [Billy Shankly] was there, I played a game and they said. ‘We'd like to sign you.' I thought, ‘It's a bit far from Glasgow…' I knew that Liverpool was a great club, I just thought it was too far away for a 15-year-old boy going down there by himself.”

Dalglish would go on to become a Celtic great, winning four Scottish league titles and four Scottish Cups before Liverpool came knocking again.

“Then in 1977, when I was 26, I'd been in South America for World Cup warm-ups with Scotland, because the World Cup was going to be in Argentina the next year,” he recalls.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“I came home, Celtic were going to Australia and I said to the manager, ‘I don't want to go.' Jock Stein said, ‘Go home and think about it.'

“I told him, ‘I have thought about it', and by the way, for me to stand up to him like that, I was terrified! I stayed at Celtic Park and trained with the reserves.

What followed next was a clear sign that Stein was preparing for life without his star player.

“When the first team came back, I played a couple of pre-season games, one at Dunfermline. We were in the dressing room, ready to go out and I was captain, but Big Jock threw the ball at one of the other players and said, ‘On you go, you take them out.'

“The rest of them were all saying to me, ‘Oh… where are *you* going?' I said, ‘I don't know!' “After the game, I dropped into my father-in-law's pub on the way home. Big Jock phoned the pub and said, ‘Right, do you still want to go?' I said, ‘Aye, boss.' He said, ‘Get yourself up here, there are two people who want to talk to you.'

“It was about 10.30pm – Bob Paisley and the chairman of Liverpool were there. About five minutes later, everything was agreed.”

For more than a decade, Joe Mewis has worked in football journalism as a reporter and editor. Mewis has had stints at Mirror Football and LeedsLive among others and worked at FourFourTwo throughout Euro 2024, reporting on the tournament. In addition to his journalist work, Mewis is also the author of four football history books that include times on Leeds United and the England national team. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.
