#1012. Sore throat? The brain has surprising control over how ill you feel

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Max Kozlov is a senior reporter with Nature in Washington DC.

Researchers are beginning to show how neurons in the brain detect an infection and tailor physiological responses to fight it.Credit: Dr. Chris Henstridge/SPL

A viral cold or bacterial infection can leave you feeling miserable, but each infection produces its own mix of symptoms. Now, neuroscientists are discovering that the brain is the conductor of these responses — decoding the type of pathogen that has invaded, accessing memories of past bouts of illness and even mobilizing immune defences at the sight of a sick person.

The findings, many of which are unpublished, were presented on 15 November at the Society for Neuroscience annual meeting in Washington DC, and challenge the established view of what it means to feel unwell. Neuroscientists have long viewed neurological responses to infection as a one-size-fits-all response to inflammation, rather than a strategy tailored to the threat.

“Sickness is actually not a fixed program, although we often talk about it this way,” said Jessica Osterhout, a neurobiologist at the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, who chaired the session.

A bacterial infection and a cold caused by a virus can both result in fever and exhaustion, yet they rarely trigger the same constellation of symptoms. Bacterial infections, for instance, tend to suppress appetite much more sharply than do colds, which made Osterhout and her colleagues wonder how the brain tells various pathogens apart.

Your brain could be controlling how sick you get — and how you recover

Your brain could be controlling how sick you get — and how you recover

In unpublished experiments, Osterhout’s team compared mice injected with a bacterial toxin with those given a compound that mimics a viral infection. To see how the brain distinguished between pathogens, the researchers profiled individual cells in circumventricular organs, which are specialized structures with unusually permeable blood vessels that surround brain ventricles.

When the body has an infection, cells in the circumventricular organs switch on sets of immune-related genes and release distinct mixes of chemical signals. Those signals diffuse to nearby neurons and create distinct patterns of activity for different pathogens, allowing the brain to customize its symptom profile depending on the threat.

Rather than acting as conduits that let inflammatory signals pass unchecked from the blood into the wider brain, these structures “may actually interpret them”, Osterhout said.

Sometimes, the brain doesn’t even wait for pathogens to enter the body to rally the immune system1. Andrea Serino, a neuroscientist at Lausanne University Hospital in Switzerland, studies how the brain maps peripersonal space, which is the area around the body roughly in arm’s reach.

When Serino’s team placed volunteers in virtual reality, they found that threat-monitoring brain regions became active when avatars bearing skin lesions caused by viral or bacterial infections approached, even when the figures were beyond arm’s reach. Just 15 minutes of virtual exposure triggered a surge in frontline immune ‘sentinel’ cells in participants’ blood comparable to that induced by an influenza vaccine. This reaction did not occur when participants saw healthy-looking avatars or ones expressing fear.

These experiments suggest that the immune system uses “the predictive ability of the brain to react before pathogens enter the body”, Serino said.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03774-w

#1011. Harry Potter films turns 25 ahead of new TV series' release

In 2001, "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone" hit cinemas and took the world by storm. Today, anticipation for the new series is high, but its creator, J.K. Rowling, remains a controversial figure.

On November 4, 2001, London's Leicester Square became a world of witches and wizards. The occasion was the world premiere of "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone" (released in the US and India as "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone").

"Thousands of excited fans, some dressed up in wizard hats and cloaks, gathered to catch a glimpse of arriving celebrities," the BBC reported at the time.

Daniel Radcliffe, who played Harry Potter, was just 12 years old and clearly impressed by the spectacle. The BBC quoted him as saying, "It is so cool. I have never heard my name shouted so much in an hour."

The crowds showed just how far Harry Potter fever had spread in only four years.

The first Harry Potter book was published by Britain's Bloomsbury in June 1997, with an initial print run of just 500 hardcover copies.

About 5,000 paperback copies were also released around the same time.

Today, first editions are prized collectors' items, with hardcover copies commanding high prices at auction. In mid-October, one sold for $400,000 through US auction house Heritage Auctions.

At first, the book's popularity grew largely by word of mouth among schoolchildren. Media attention followed when it won the prestigious Nestle Smarties Book Prize later that year.

With an estimated 120 million-plus copies sold worldwide, it is the best-selling book in the series and ranks among the best-selling novels of all time.

For years, J.K. Rowling's public image was defined by her extraordinary rise from a single mother on welfare to a billionaire.

But in recent years, debate over her views on gender and transgender identity has increasingly overshadowed that success. It's an issue Rowling herself frequently weighs in on.

In an essay published on her website on October 21, 2026, Rowling reiterated her opposition to what she calls the "current, dominant strain of trans activism." She argues that this movement "holds that a man who declares himself a woman is, literally, a woman, and is therefore entitled to be treated as a woman in all contexts." Rowling argues that allowing trans women into single-sex spaces poses a risk. She describes biological sex as an indisputable biological fact.

Such statements have led critics to accuse Rowling of transphobia, while others regard her stance as a defense of women's rights and safety.

The controversy has also divided her fans. Some stand by Rowling, while others try to draw a distinction between the books and their author.

Others have left Harry Potter behind altogether. One former fan is German YouTuber Coldmirror, known for her Harry Potter parodies. The media artist from the Bremen area, whose real name is Kathrin Fricke, told the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper: "I don't have any love left for Harry. I'm still somewhat interested, but I can no longer watch it in good conscience." She cited Rowling's campaigning against transgender people as the reason.

The "Harry Potter" film cast is divided as well. The three main stars — Daniel Radcliffe, Emma Watson and Rupert Grint — have publicly spoken out in support of transgender people. Meanwhile, Ralph Fiennes, who played Lord Voldemort, and Helena Bonham Carter, who portrayed Bellatrix Lestrange, have defended Rowling's right to express her views.

Despite the controversy surrounding Rowling, Warner Bros., which holds the Harry Potter film rights, is bringing the books back to the screen — this time as a series for HBO. The premiere is scheduled for December 25.

The eight-episode first season is an an adaption of the first book. Even though the episode lengths haven't been announced, the scope of a TV series gives each book much more room than the original films did. That means more time to explore subplots, character development and everyday life at Hogwarts. While many fans are looking forward to a more detailed adaptation, others remain skeptical. They find it hard to imagine the familiar characters being played by anyone else.

The new trio consists of Dominic McLaughlin as Harry Potter, Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger and Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley.

J.K. Rowling is an executive producer on the show. HBO says, however, that her views on gender identity won't be reflected in the storyline. Several people involved in the new production have publicly distanced themselves from her views. Paapa Essiedu, who has been cast as Severus Snape, signed an open letter supporting transgender people. Rowling subsequently said she had neither the power nor the desire to have him removed from the show because of it. John Lithgow, who plays Dumbledore, and Nick Frost, who portrays Hagrid, have also spoken out against Rowling's views.

Meanwhile, the Harry Potter merchandising machine is still going strong. On November 4, Britain's largest Harry Potter store to date is set to open in London. According to Warner Bros., the two-story shop covers more than 1,950 square meters.

This article was originally written in German.

#1010. Aitana Bonmatí makes Guardian top 100 history with third title in a row

The margin may have got smaller but the brilliant Spanish midfielder makes it a hat-trick of No 1 finishes

They say the best things come in threes, and Aitana Bonmatí has written herself into the Guardian’s top 100 history as the first player to finish at the top of the tree for a third consecutive year.

Last year the majestic midfielder emulated her Barcelona and Spain teammate Alexia Putellas by winning for a second year running, but the 27-year-old has now gone one better, establishing herself once again at the top of the women’s game.

As the Top 100 approaches a decade since its inception, nobody has quite dominated an era like Bonmatí and, while 2025 did not end in major silverware on the European stage, there were moments of sublime brilliance on the way to a Champions League final as well as the Euro one with Spain.

Bonmatí, as the very best do, has become a figure who can step up when needed most, and has become synonymous with the Blaugrana Barcelona stripes, a one-club woman with over 300 appearances in all competitions for the Catalan giants. Catalonia born and bred, both her parents were teachers of the Catalan language, with Bonmatí’s life and career intertwined with the region since she was a child, and now she has become an icon not just at home, but all around the world.

In a time where the women’s game is growing exponentially and world class talents are queueing up to dethrone the midfielder, she remains at the top. However, having broken a leg in training before the Nations League final she will miss more than four months of 2026. She will be sorely missed.

It was a tighter margin of victory in 2025, 453 points ahead of compatriot Mariona Caldentey – compared to 568 last year ahead of Caroline Graham Hansen – with the Spanish duo plus Alessia Russo and Putellas all gaining over 4,000 points from our record panel of 143 judges.

Bonmatí received 43% of the No 1 votes, ahead of Caldentey with a 21% share. Russo and Putellas both had 8% of the first picks in third and fourth respectively.

In a year where England backed up their Euro 2022 success with victory in Switzerland, Brazil continued their dominance in South America and Nigeria regained supremacy in Africa, it was all change across the top 100 as players such as Caldentey, Russo, Hannah Hampton, Temwa Chawinga, Patri Guijarro, Ewa Pajor and Clàudia Pina all made a new-look top 10 for the first time.

The Barcelona starlet Pina was the biggest mover, up 65 places on 2024, followed by another Spaniard in Gotham FC striker Esther González, up 59, while Klara Bühl moved up 40, just ahead of Russo’s 39 to propel the Arsenal striker into the top three.

Ghizlane Chebbak gave Morocco a first ever entry into the top 100 and Canada’s new Northern Super League was represented in its first year thanks to the Nigerian striker Esther Okoronkwo of AFC Toronto.

In fact, almost a quarter of this year’s 100 were brand new faces, emphasising just how fast the women’s game is growing, with the Chelsea and England shot-stopper Hampton the highest of the new names, shooting straight into the top five after her Euro-winning performances, while Vicky López, Sofia Cantore, Nathalie Björn and Michelle Agyemang all made the top 50.

Performances on the continental stage earned first-time appearances for the likes of Okoronkwo, Brazil’s Amanda Gutierres and Nigeria’s Gift Monday, while potential stars of the future such as Olivia Smith, Lily Yohannes and Signe Gaupset ranked for the first time. Mexico’s Charlyn Corral gained long overdue recognition.

Others made their way back into the 100, such as the Arsenal and England duo Leah Williamson and Chloe Kelly after a trophy-laden 12 months while Sandy Baltimore and Cristiana Girelli also made returns straight into the top quarter.

Lucy Bronze, Wendie Renard and Pernille Harder remain the only three players to have maintained a place every year after Saki Kumagai and Jenni Hermoso dropped out for the first time and it was Bronze’s Chelsea who dethroned Barcelona as the team with the most representatives with 15 compared to Arsenal’s 14 and Barcelona’s 12 after a domestic treble for Sonia Bompastor’s side.

Unsurprisingly after another Euro success, England pip Spain as the nation with the most players, 14 to 13, followed by the USA and France with nine each, while Copa América winners Brazil move into the top five for the first time with five players of their own.

The Women’s Super League asserts its dominance with 39 players on the list, up 12 from 2024, ahead of the NWSL with 19 and Liga F with 16. Players such as Jess Park, Aoba Fujino, Mary Fowler and Maya Le Tissier just missed out.

The young and old were once again represented at either end of the spectrum, with Marta again the oldest representative, the 39-year-old playing a key role in Brazil’s Copa América success with a dramatic late goal in the final against Colombia to keep their hopes alive. The OL Lyonnes and USA superstar Yohannes is the youngest at 18 and one of three teenagers to rank alongside López and Agyemang.

But it is again Bonmatí who ranks above them all, asserting her authority as one of the greatest of the modern era.

Rushden was a TV newcomer when he landed the top job on Sky’s iconic football show

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For a generation of football fans in the UK, Soccer AM was a staple of their Saturday morning routine.

The Sky TV show combined football, comedy and celebrity guests, all with a healthy dose of general chaos.

When TV newcomer and longtime Soccer AM fan Max Rushden landed the co-presenter job alongside Helen Chamberlain in 2008, he was thrown into a world he had never experienced before.

“Getting the job was mad because I'd never done a TV show in my life, and it definitely showed in the first two years,” Rushden tells FourFourTwo.

“But I loved the show – I was a fan of the week in 2000 and watched it religiously until about two or three years before getting the job, so the whole thing was surreal.”

Rushden’s journey from avid viewer to presenter had plenty of twists, including an audition for another iconic British TV programme.

“I was doing a breakfast show on Radio London, but I had to go back to reading the news because I wasn't famous,” he continues.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“I thought, ‘OK, I'll make a show and send it to everybody' – the only two people who replied were from the Travel Channel, who said I was boring, and Sky Sports, who asked me to go in for a chat.

“I bowled in, chatted about Cambridge and Soccer AM for an hour. They said they might have something for me in a couple of months, but I didn't expect much.”

After leaving the audition with low expectations, Rushden continued to explore other possibilities.

“In the meantime, I'd got an audition for Blue Peter,” he reveals before receiving a life-changing telephone call.

“Before I went to it, I got a call from Sky and they asked, “Do you want to do Soccer AM?” My head just exploded and I was trying to play it cool.

"I signed the contract and s**t myself for a month before the show started.”

#1006. Gold for the West Bank: Meet Palestinian karate champ Mariam Bsharat

The occupied West Bank is not an obvious breeding ground for sporting success. But Mariam Bsharat, 17, has beaten the odds to become a karate world champion and is making a new life in Germany.

"After the referee lifted my hand to show I'm now a two-time world champion, it was a very overwhelming feeling," Mariam Bsharat said. "Making history once is something, but making it twice is really something else. I felt very happy and I felt a big relief. Only I know how many sacrifices I made and how many hardships I needed to overcome."

Themes of relief, joy and sacrifice are commonplace in the reflections of athletes after a big win. In Mariam Bsharat's case, it's about more than just dedication to training and taking care of the body. The 17-year-old won her second under-21 World Karate Championship gold medal competing for the Palestine national team in Poland in October.

"It was everyday life, seeing people get killed around me and houses getting bombed," she told DW of her upbringing in the occupied West Bank.

"I faced challenges in transportation," Bsharat said. "I wasn't able to go from one city to another to be able to train with other people, so that I can actually prepare for competitions. I needed to travel to other countries like Jordan or Egypt ... which was very hard for me. And, financially, the support wasn't really the support an elite athlete needed."

Growing up in Nablus, Bsharat had a narrow path to the top. But initially, it was her own reluctance that threatened to stop a champion career before it started.

"When I was a little kid, I did not really love it," said Bsharat, who competes in the division for fighters who weigh under 66 kilograms (145 pounds).

"I started it because my family was in that sport," Bsharat said. "My father had a dojo, and my mother also did that sport. My siblings and my aunts and my uncles — it's a family thing. I started it because they were all doing it. In time, I started getting into it."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Family has been a constant source of comfort and inspiration for Bsharat. Her father and uncle have acted as manager and coach respectively. While her mother and siblings moved with Mariam to Hamburg, Germany, last year, her father remained in order to take care of his business, the dojo, though he visits and tries to be with his daughter in competitions. Integration has been made easier by her mastery of the language, taught to her by her German mother.

Bsharat has mixed feelings about leaving her homeland.

"I'm thankful to be here because being in Germany opened lot of doors for me, and I think I have a brighter future here," Bsharat said. "But also being in Palestine was just my everyday life, and I loved it there. My family was around me, my friends were around me, and I just felt comfortable, which was a big change coming here to Germany. I think every change comes with hardships."

As well as the obvious difficulties of living in an area occupied by Israel, there are particular challenges for sportspeople living in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip, with access to facilities, travel and constant security fears among them. As such, very few people from the Palestinian territories become successful on the international sporting stage. That, Bsharat said, gives her responsibilities that are unusual and heavy for a person of any age, let alone a 17-year-old.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Being an elite athlete in Palestine is something very special because not everybody in Palestine has that opportunity. There aren't really a lot of athletes that are elite and who win international medals,” Bsharat said.

"So all that pressure from all the country and all the people, the family, the coaches are on me because I'm representing them, raising their flag,” she said. "I sometimes even forget to fight for myself and actually think about myself."

That has not yet proved a barrier to Bsharat, who is is ranked first in the world in her category by the World Karate Federation (WKF). With Palestine recognized by the International Olympic Committee, Bsharat would likely have been a contender to raise that flag in Los Angeles at the 2028 Olympics. But the sport was dropped from the Games in 2024.

"The global karate community remains steadfast in our belief that the natural place for karate is within the Olympic Games, and we sincerely hope that the incongruence we suffered in Paris 2024 and LA 2028 will be corrected for Brisbane 2032, if not sooner," the WKF wrote in response to the decision in 2024. The sport was also taken off the slate for the recent Youth Games in Senegal.

Should karate return in Brisbane, Bsharat would likely be approaching her prime. In the meantime, she is looking forward to starting her journey as a senior when she turns 18. But she won't be hanging around.

"My goal is it to be a world champion at seniors, which is the hardest and the best thing you can achieve in karate," she said.

"But winning an Olympic medal, being called Olympic champion or just representing my country with that flag [is a thought that] is just full of happiness and pride."

The interview was conducted by Janek Speight.

#1005. Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top

The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals

What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature. My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career.

After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure.

Based on those answers, one player stood out above all the others: a kid called Ousmane Dembélé, then a youth player yet to make a first-team appearance at Rennes. Eleven years after appearing in these pages as one to watch, Dembélé has been voted the best male player in the world by the Guardian’s 219-strong voting panel.

Those intangible qualities were in full effect on the night Dembélé made good on his years of promise. The defining image of Paris Saint-Germain’s 5-0 win over Inter in the 2025 Champions League final was not the trophy lift, or any one of the goal celebrations, but Dembélé, poised on the edge of the opposition penalty area, with hunched demeanour and furrowed brow, his face a picture of focus, ready to press. Just how did he get to this point?

One lesson to learn from the Dembélé story: the path to greatness is not always linear. He started off like a train, winning France’s young player of the year award in his first season as a professional. The following season, he helped Borussia Dortmund win the German Cup.

Around that time, in the course of research for my book, Edge, I spoke to Thomas Tuchel, his coach at Dortmund. Tuchel told me that Dembélé’s talent came with an obligation and responsibility to improve. He bracketed his players into one of three “ABC” categories, depending on their dominant motivation, and would change his man-management style accordingly.

The A category stood for “aggressive-motivated”, and referred to players motivated by individual glory and awards (in Tuchel’s eyes, this was not necessarily a negative: think Neymar at Paris).

B stood for “binding-motivated”, those players who love being part of the group and bringing people together (often captains, such as César Azpilicueta at Chelsea).

C stood for “curious-motivated”. These were the players capable of greatness, who needed to be trained in a slightly different way. Their talent could take them far; and on a good day, they were capable of anything. Tuchel loved coaching these players. Dembélé, he felt, was a C.

But the journey was not always smooth. In 2017, he moved to Barcelona, who were flush with money from selling Neymar for €222m (£194m). It was a sliding doors moment. That same summer, Barcelona changed coach: in came Ernesto Valverde; out went Luis Enrique. In six injury-laden years at Barcelona, Dembélé started only a third of the league games. He scored a total of 24 league goals. His most memorable moment might have been missing a last-minute one-on-one in the 2019 Champions League semi-final against Liverpool, when Barcelona were already 3-0 up (remember what happened next? They lost the second leg 4-0). When he did leave, amid mutterings of wasted talent and blackmail, it felt like a relief for all parties.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

There is some symmetry to Dembélé’s exceptional 2025. Of the 30 goals he has scored this calendar year at the time of writing, the most decisive and emblematic was probably against Liverpool in the second leg of their Champions League last-16 tie. With PSG 1-0 down from the first leg, Dembélé drifted into his own half, losing his markers who didn’t want to follow him that far. He picked up the ball and spread it wide to the right-winger Bradley Barcola, then sprinted into the box and made it to the cross to score. (He also scored a penalty in PSG’s successful shootout after they won 1-0 at Anfield that night). Dembélé did something similar against Arsenal in the semi-final, dropping deep early in the game, switching the play to the left-sided Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and receiving the return ball, unmarked, on the edge of the area, before scoring. Even when teams knew it was coming, they couldn’t stop him.

At the start of last season, Luis Enrique’s plan was for the whole team to replace the goals of Kylian Mbappé, who had joined Real Madrid. After all, Dembélé had not scored more than 10 league goals in a season since his debut campaign at Rennes. Luis Enrique wanted the team to be the star. And so, with no star player to serve, Dembélé was liberated. This curious-motivated talent who once scored penalties with either foot, and even took corners with either foot, quietly became the main man. He starts the press; his vision, movement, pace, control and positioning set the tone; and his finishing, once considered wasteful, is ruthless.

I still don’t know exactly what makes a good player great but I am closer to an answer. Part of the equation remains what we cannot see: the chemistry within a team, the relationship with a specific coach, playing in a system that brings out the best in every player. But also those other qualities that Dembélé had at 17, and still has now. This well-deserved prize is as much for those attributes as it is for his goals and the trophies he helped Paris Saint-Germain win.

This backing helped Bogle’s side win promotion back to the Premier League in the right-back’s first season in West Yorkshire, which was followed up by a respectable 14th-place finish back in the top flight last term.

The Leeds fanbase has taken its fair share of knocks over the years, and while Bogle knows just how important building this authentic connection with the fans is, it has to be done in the right way.

#1001. What the Democrats' midterms win means for the US economy and Trump

From high oil prices and data centers to tariffs and mounting debt, economic concerns played a key role in the crushing defeat of President Donald Trump's Republicans. So can the Democrats now make a difference?

For the millions who cast their ballots in the US midterm elections, one issue ranked above all others: the economy.

So what does the Democrats' stunning capture of both the US Senate and House of Representatives mean for the economy and economic policy, given that President Donald Trump still has two years of his term to go?

Markets have rebounded after initially trending negatively. Global stocks rallied as investors appeared to take heart from the Democrats' victory.

With Democrats now holding comfortable majorities in both houses of Congress and Trump still in the White House, it could lead to gridlock in Washington. Trump has already said he would become "Mr Veto," meaning he would block any legislation the Democrats advance.

"The magnitude of the gains for the Democrats in the midterms does not change too much for the near-term policy outlook, given the party still lacks a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate and President Trump has veto power to block legislation," Stephen Brown, chief North America economist with Capital Economics, said in a note.

"I think we are looking at two years of complete 100% gridlock," Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, nonresident senior fellow with the Peterson Institute for International Economics, told DW after the results came in. "Nothing will get done of any kind."

Some investors appear worried that the Democrats could force through AI regulation, especially if they also win the White House in 2028. Rising opposition among large majorities of the US population to data centers — the key infrastructure behind AI — helped secure victories for many Democratic candidates.

Kirkegaard, who is also a senior fellow at Bruegel, a European economics think tank, said the vote showed the extent of that opposition.  Even if the Democrats can't force regulation, he thinks local opposition will make it harder for data centers to be built, which could hit the valuation of big tech firms that have benefitted from the AI boom.

"This election shows that the political underpinning of the rapid, aggressive AI growth story is shaky," he said. "It doesn't mean it's going to stop or be made illegal, but the dynamic of the growth story has shifted."

If the Democrats were to win the presidency in 2028, Brown said, they would be perfectly placed to make major policy changes. "That includes the potential for tax hikes on corporations and high-income individuals as well as regulation that could delay the AI rollout," he said.

According to polling conducted in early October by the Pew Research Center, 56% of Americans say Trump's tariff policies will have mostly negative impacts on the country, with only 20% saying mostly positive.

That sentiment clearly drove many Democrats to victory in the midterms — particularly in states where tariffs have had a particularly negative impact. That includes those with sectors reliant on exports, such as Texas, Michigan, Iowa and Illinois, where counter-tariffs have hit and those that have high trade volumes with Canada.

Yet, barring an unprecedented climbdown from Trump — who has been ideologically wedded to tariffs since he first became a public figure almost 50 years ago — it's not clear how the Democrats could force substantial change to the president's signature economic policy.

"Trump will not be moderated," Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation in Singapore, told DW earlier this year. "Expect him to continue his trade disruption and tariff policies for as long as he remains in the Oval Office."

Though the US Constitution gives Congress the power to collect and organize tariffs, various laws passed over the years have given presidents power to implement tariffs when they cite certain conditions, such as national security or economic emergencies.

Trump has already used such avenues for his tariffs and can continue to do so, despite some legal rebukes. However, while Congress can't necessarily force an end to Trump's existing tariffs, it can now take further legal action against them to prevent greater escalation.

Though Trump and the Democrats are clearly not going to make common cause, Kirkegaard said, the scale of the Republicans' defeat might force Trump to be less erratic in his policymaking, from escalating his trade war with Canada to his Iran policy.

Trump said in the aftermath of Tuesday's defeats that he would "work with" the Democrats and told the Financial Times in the run-up to the vote that he was unlikely to escalate the war in Iran.

Were a deal to be struck with Iran, soaring energy prices — a pivotal election issue — could finally fall, helping voters with their cost-of-living concerns.

"You've got to get a deal with Iran, and you've got to bring down gas prices," Kirkegaard said. "From a political point of view, that's the most important thing now."

George Saravelos, an analyst with Deutsche Bank FX Research, thinks the markets are beginning to become more optimistic in that area. "With oil flows through the Middle East having materially recovered, the market is pricing a large imminent risk premium of re-escalation and energy supply disruption," he said in a note.

Despite the scale of the Democrats' victory, the fact that Trump remains in the Oval Office will complicate all efforts to force a change to signature economic policies and issues.

Yet Congress can now exert considerable pressure. Another issue vital to voters was corruption and the belief that the Trump administration has engaged in corruption and personal enrichment while in office.

That raises the prospect of the new Democratic-controlled Congress launching legal investigations and potentially pursuing another impeachment of Trump, which could force the president to negotiate on some economic issues to secure his political survival.

"Can you find 10 or 12 Republican senators who, in the face of overwhelming corruption, would be willing to vote for articles of impeachment? I wouldn't rule it out," Kirkegaard said. "And that's a scenario in which Trump might suddenly be much more accommodating to, for instance, abandoning most of his tariffs."

Despite voters' clear rejection of Trump's economic policies, the Democratic Party's newly minted senators, congressmen and congresswomen face an uphill battle in trying to reverse them.

#1000. Which football club has had most international captains in the same team? | The Knowledge

Plus: more speedy marathons by footballers, headed goals of the season and chairs acting as managers

Mail us with all of your questions and answers

“Which club team has had the most international captains playing together at one time?” asks MH Zahid. “Conversely, which international team has had the most club captains in its starting lineup at one time?”

A quick web search finds a fuss being made in various corners of the internet of Chelsea’s 2009-10 squad because it contained six national team captains in Michael Ballack (Germany), Petr Cech (Czech Republic), Didier Drogba (Côte d’Ivoire), Branislav Ivanovic (Serbia), Mikel John Obi (Nigeria) and John Terry (England). These are, indeed, six people who captained their countries, playing together at one time, but crucially they were not all international captains at that time, which because we like to have our hands bound as tight as possible – no questions please – mean they are disqualified from this particular tournament. Ivanovic, you see, was not named Serbia captain until 2012 and Mikel, who was but a whippersnapper at 22 when the 2009-10 season started, was still seven years from getting his hands on the Nigeria armband.

But if that Chelsea team are not themselves the best answer that Knowledge has come up with, they are at least associated with them, having been knocked out of the Champions League by José Mourinho’s captain-strewn Inter. Inter ended up beating Bayern Munich 2-0 in the final, with a team that included the then full-time captains of Brazil (Lúcio), Romania (Cristian Chivu), Cameroon (Samuel Eto’o) and Macedonia (Goran Pandev), while the captain of Serbia (Dejan Stankovic) came off the bench to replace Chivu in the second half and Pandev was replaced by Sulley Muntari, who while not Ghana’s full-time captain had led the side in their most recent game, a 2-1 defeat at Bosnia and Herzegovina that March.

But that’s not all! Among the unused substitutes was Iván Córdoba, who at this point in his career had lost Colombia’s armband to Mario Yepes but been given it back for their previous game, against Paraguay, in the absence of his fellow centre-back. Also in the team and worthy of note, if not of inclusion in our tally of then captains, were Wesley Sneijder, occasional Netherlands skipper and still their all-time record appearance maker, and Javier Zanetti, who regularly captained Argentina and is No 4 on their list of all-time appearance makers (he would be higher had he not been frozen out by their then manager, Diego Maradona, before the 2010 World Cup), with occasional Kenya captain McDonald Mariga also among the subs.

By our count that’s seven players in one matchday squad who could boast of being their country’s current captain at kick-off, and none of whom captained their club side – that honour went to Zanetti. Our searches have not found another team to match that one, but readers have suggested a couple who came close, in the shape of Tottenham in 2020-21 (who boasted five international captains at the time in Hugo Lloris of France; Serge Aurier of Côte d’Ivoire; South Korea’s Son Heung-min; Gareth Bale of Wales; and England’s own Harry Kane, suggested by John Curry) and Liverpool just last year, when in Conor Bradley, Andy Robertson, Virgil van Dijk, Wataru Endo, Mo Salah and Dominik Szoboszlai they had six – though they never played together while they were all incumbent international captains. Any more for any more?

The fastest former footballer we found in time for last week’s instalment was Alexei Smertin, the former Russia and Chelsea midfielder, who screamed around the Kazan Marathon course in 2020 in just two hours, 48 minutes and 17 seconds. But as Richard Askham emailed to point out, that has since been bettered by Joe Skarz, formerly of Bury, Rotherham and Oxford United, and current manager of Golcar United of the Northern Counties East League Premier Division, who in 2025 finished the Yorkshire Marathon with a chip time of 2hr 47min 33sec.

The next question is what level of football do you need to reach to qualify as a footballer? Because Stig Lindmark tipped us off about the former AIK academy player Andreas Almgren, whose dreams of football glory were derailed by injury in his teens and eventually shifted his focus towards distance running. In New York at the start of this month – while the retired cyclist Tom Dumoulin was putting most former footballers to shame with a time of 2:27:12 – he ran his first ever marathon and only went and won the thing, in 2hr 6min 1sec. With no senior competitive appearances he probably does not count, but it’s a good enough effort to get a mention.

“Has a headed goal ever been awarded goal of the season,” wonders Rupert Sheard. “I can think of a few belters, but awards tend to go to ones kicked in.”

“The closest I could get was Robin van Persie’s flying header at the 2014 World Cup in Brazil, for the Netherlands against Spain,” writes Sinan Eccles. “He was pipped to the official goal of the tournament by James Rodríguez’s iconic volley, but did make it to third in that year’s Puskas Award – behind Rodríguez and Stephanie Roche.”

Peter Tomlin writes: “Having researched the goal of the season awards in many countries, the only header I could find that won was Keith Houchen’s fantastic one in the 1986-87 FA Cup Final for Coventry v Tottenham. However, Alisson’s dramatic 95th-minute headed winner v West Brom was voted Liverpool’s goal of the season for the 2020-21 season.”

And Mark Johnson points out that Basile Boli’s ridiculous bullet header for Marseille against PSG at the end of the 1993 season would surely have won the Ligue 1 goal of the season award but for the inconvenient fact that no such award existed at the time.

Martyn Amos has responded to last week’s scepticism about the possibility of an Ipswich fan website existing in 1990, the year before the first known website went online. “Just to clarify, the original page was set up by Phil Clarke, who was working at BT Labs in Martlesham (near Ipswich), in 1990,” he writes. “At the time, as I said, the web was still experimental, and I think the page was only available internally. Your correspondent is correct in saying that the first public website appeared in August 1991. But the ITFC page still existed, in some recognisable form, using the standard web technology, in 1990, so I think it counts. That’s my understanding, anyway.”

With Lee Power taking charge of Swindon Town, in last week’s Knowledge archive we dug up our piece from 2006 on chairs acting as managers, we wrote in October 2015. Neil Bellis, the director of communications at Chester FC, writes to point out we missed Terry Smith off our list.

“He took over four games into the season despite not really knowing much about ‘soccer’,” writes Neil. “He was a former American Football coach but for some reason ending up buying our club. Not only did we end up getting relegated from the Football League for the first time in 1999-2000 we also saw a few very strange ideas from him including having a team talk as the Lord’s prayer and appointing a captain in defence, midfield and attack. Thankfully we are now fan owned so this level of insanity shouldn’t happen again.”

One of Smith’s first games as manager was against Aston Villa in the League Cup, a fixture that prompted a visit from ITV to see what was going on. The result of that visit can be seen here:

“There’s nothing magical about being a coach,’ said Smith not long after his arrival. “It’s like being the general manager of a business, the coaching principles are the same in any sport.” That doesn’t sound too promising but things didn’t really go horribly wrong until the end of November, when Chester began a run of 11 defeats in 12 matches. There’s some footage here of the aftermath of the 5-1 home defeat by Leyton Orient just after Christmas – “I want to thank you guys,” says Smith in the dressing room. “That’s the most pitiful, pitiful effort I’ve ever damn seen.”

Smith stepped down as manager and brought in Ian Atkins in January 2000, then sold the club in October 2001.

“What’s the highest score by a team or in a match where no player scored more than one goal?” writes Paul Gage.

“Manchester United have 20 league titles, won by three managers. Liverpool have 20 league titles won by 10. Which teams have the most and fewest titles won by the most and fewest managers?” asks Will Marquand.

“Djed Spence (shirt No 99) set up Pio Esposito (No 94) in Inter’s 2-0 win over Como at the weekend. Has there ever been a combination for a goal (assist and scorer) with a higher combined shirt number than 193?” writes Joe Strawson.

“Did the Fenerbahce side have more combined Premier League appearances than Liverpool in the teams’ recent Champions League match? If so was this the first instance of a club in Europe playing opposition who had more game appearances in their own league than they had themselves?” ponders Josh Wolff-Martin.

#999. WSL talking points: Chelsea’s gamble pays off and have Arsenal lost fear factor?

Blues beat champions after bold substitution and Gunners’ home struggles continue with fifth consecutive WSL draw

Sonia Bompastor attempted to deflect suggestions that the removal of Kadeisha Buchanan 12 minutes into Chelsea’s top-of-the-table clash with Manchester City was tactical, but few were convinced by the claim that it was down to injury. The manager said the centre-back, who had not asked to come off and walked straight down the tunnel, had taken a knock to the head in training and been assessed and cleared, but that during the game “she was not herself”. On came Veerle Buurman and the threat of Khadija Shaw was nullified, the Dutch defender restricting the golden boot favourite so well that Shaw did not manage a shot on target. Bompastor said after the game that she had not spoken to Buchanan but that she would “explain myself to her”. “I always have good relationships with the players, bring them clarity, and I’m always direct and honest so they have the information,” she said. “It won’t be any different.” Enforced or not, the substitution was a huge gamble that paid off, even after the loss of Melvine Malard to injury in the first half reduced their number of remaining in-game substitution windows to one. Suzanne Wrack

Match report: Chelsea 1-0 Manchester City

Manchester United earned their fourth clean sheet in all competitions in their 2-0 defeat of Crystal Palace. Maya Le Tissier stole the headlines with her goal on her 150th appearance for the club but the team’s improved defensive stability is also catching the eye and the centre-back is key to that. “For a defender you expect as the minimum you need to defend well and help to build,” said the head coach, Eva Olid. “But now she’s scoring goals and that is more than a manager can ask from a centre-back. She’s in a high level and I’m so happy for her.” Le Tissier is showing consistent solidity and appears to be enjoying life under Olid now that things have settled, after seven goals conceded in their opening two WSL games. United have conceded four in eight WSL games since and are starting to show their flair. SW

Have teams stopped fearing Arsenal at the Emirates Stadium? Their run of five consecutive WSL draws at home suggests so. London City Lionesses had 56% possession on Sunday and controlled the game for significant spells, especially in the second half, and although Arsenal created the greater chances, they do not play with the aura of a side attracting the largest attendances in the division. Renée Slegers was asked whether she was worried her team were losing that home “fear factor” and said: “No, because we love playing at the Emirates. We had the biggest crowd so far in the season, the atmosphere was fantastic under the lights.” Probed further about her side’s home form, the head coach said: “I don’t think we’ve lost the fear factor, I think it’s a very hard place for oppositions to come.” Her side host West Ham next Sunday, looking for that elusive home WSL win. Tom Garry

Tottenham Hotspur were the latest team frustrated by Everton’s defensive solidity as they were held to a goalless draw. Despite controlling the ball and registering 17 shots, only three efforts were on target as they failed to score for the first time. Martin Ho was keen to highlight their opponents’ strengths as a key reason. “When we got into that attacking third, it was going to take something really special,” he told Spursplay. “They defended so deep with so many numbers behind the ball. You’re waiting for one of those moments to drop.” It was just the kind of performance fans have come to expect from Scott Phelan’s side. Unbeaten in their past three, in which they have faced Manchester United, Chelsea and Spurs, Everton have developed a strong resilience and character in recent weeks. Where they struggle is at the other end. Everton have scored eight goals this season (three of them own goals), higher than only Charlton in the WSL. Sophie Downey

Liverpool ended their five-game winless league run with a statement victory over struggling Brighton, their third away win in 17 games. It has been a frustrating October and November block for Gareth Taylor and his team so there was much relief on the sideline that they were finally able to turn performance and opportunity into three points. Liverpool had less of the ball but their fast counterattacking proved too much for the Seagulls. A significant key to their success was Beata Olsson. She has six goals from her past five games in all competitions, stepping up when her team have needed it most. Injuries have kept out Aurélie Csillag and Ceri Holland for the best part of the season and Sophie Roman Haug is recovering from an anterior cruciate ligament injury sustained 13 months ago. With limited attacking options, therefore, it will be very welcome that the Swedish striker has found her form in front of goal. SD

Viviane Asseyi continued her impressive scoring form with a superb brace in West Ham’s 2-0 victory over Charlton, taking her WSL tally to seven this season. The striker opened the scoring with a composed finish from the edge of the area before producing the standout moment of the afternoon, curling a spectacular 25-yard free-kick into the top corner beyond Charlton’s goalkeeper, Anna Koivunen. Asseyi could have completed a hat-trick but her two goals proved decisive. West Ham’s head coach, Rita Guarino, described her as “an important player”, adding that Asseyi was in a good goalscoring spell. Guarino felt Asseyi could have been happier with a hat-trick, but her latest double underlines her importance to West Ham’s attacking threat. Mitul Samji

Poor officiating dominated the narrative of the second city derby as Aston Villa edged Birmingham City 1-0, with both sides feeling hard done by. First, City felt Lucy Parker had fouled Océane Hurtré in the penalty area in the 24th minute, only for the referee to award a corner. Whether the incident was inside the box was disputable, but it did appear to be a foul. Minutes later, Villa had a goal from Océane Deslandes overruled for what was declared a foul on the goalkeeper in another contentious call, but they managed to find a winner in the second half. The decisions added to growing concerns about consistency in the WSL. Ho recently suggested officiating had worsened, and matches such as this do little to ease those concerns. Before VAR is introduced, improving the quality of refereeing must be a priority to avoid undermining the league’s standards and progress. Réshma Rao

#998. University students are biggest spreaders of COVID

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Heidi Ledford reports for Nature from Seattle, Washington.

Undergraduate students on university campuses played a big part in spreading viral variants during the COVID-19 pandemic.Credit: Leonard Ortiz/Digital First Media/Orange County Register/Getty

Universities have become hotbeds of SARS-CoV-2 transmission, according to a massive analysis of more than 85,000 viral genome sequences and other data collected from people with COVID-19.

COVID can wake up a slew of dormant viruses inside you

COVID can wake up a slew of dormant viruses inside you

The study, published on 19 November in the journal Cell1, finds that viral transmission between 2021 and 2023 was highest in adolescents aged 15–18 in schools, undergraduates at university and residents in nursing facilities. Undergraduates, in particular, were consistently the first group to start spreading emerging genetic variants of SARS-CoV-2.

Surprisingly, however, staff members at all three types of institution had about the same risk of contracting COVID-19 as did those in their surrounding communities. So, for example, professors were about as likely to get COVID-19 from the coffee baristas in their university towns as they were to get it from a student at their university.

The analysis is among the largest to bring together viral genomic sequences and medical data from people with COVID-19. “The scale is truly impressive,” says Bill Hanage, who studies the evolution of infectious diseases at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health in Boston, Massachusetts. “It’s an example of the depth and the detail of the picture that can be painted using the medium of population genomics.”

The findings were based on data collected from COVID-19 tests taken by people in Massachusetts between November 2021 and January 2023. The genomic data allowed researchers to trace the path of SARS-CoV-2 variants that emerged over time, and to link this with epidemiological data about the study participants, such as their age and whether they had been vaccinated against COVID-19.

COVID jabs for kids: they’re safe and they work — so why is uptake so patchy?

COVID jabs for kids: they’re safe and they work — so why is uptake so patchy?

Overall, the team found that booster vaccinations helped to reduce SARS-CoV-2 transmission. This was true even for BA.1, an Omicron variant that started to circulate in Massachusetts in late 2021 — a striking result because COVID-19 vaccines at that time hadn’t yet been updated to protect against BA.1, Hanage says. “That’s an important illustration of how vaccines, even when they’re not perfect, can still be beneficial,” he says.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03746-0

#997. Cristiano Ronaldo announces retirement from international football

The announcement by the footballing legend comes just weeks after a public spat with Portugal coach Jorge Jesus over playing time.

Cristiano Ronaldo took to social media on Thursday to announce that he had played his last game for Portugal.

"To the Portuguese people, the day has come for me to hand back the No. 7 shirt of our national team," the 41-year-old Ronaldo said in a video on his Instagram account.

"I never felt it belonged to me alone, but for 23 years I had the privilege and the responsibility of wearing it, defending it and carrying it with me into stadiums all around the world," Ronaldo said.

The former Manchester United, Real Madrid and Juventus forward represented his country 234 times, scoring 146 goals — making him the men's record-holder for ⁠international ​appearances and for international goals.

He captained Portugal ​to their first major trophy at ​Euro 2016 and led them to the 2019 and 2025 Nations League titles.

"It was not an easy decision, there are decisions that are not ​only with the head. They are also made with the heart," Ronaldo continued in the Instagram post.

"If I ever made you happy, ​if one of my goals ever made you hug someone, forget a worry or feel ⁠proud ​of our country, then it ​was all worth it."

He also thanked his family, the Portuguese people ​and the teammates, coaches and staff he worked with over his national ​team career.

The Portuguese Football Association (FPF) released a statement expressing its gratitude and respect for the player also known as "CR7."

"Cristiano Ronaldo has raised Portugal's profile and inspired generations of young people who dream of following in his footsteps; for many of us, he is the greatest player of all time!" it read.

The FPF intends to organize a tribute "in which the fans and the country can one more time applaud and celebrate a player who has given us so much."

While his long-rival Lionel Messi ended his Argentina career with a much anticipated farewell match last month, Ronaldo's final appearance may go down as Portugal's 1-0 win over Wales on September 24, depending on the nature of the tribute. Portugal coach Jorge Jesus left him on the bench for the following match and said he wouldn't start the next one.

Ronaldo responded by walking out of the Portugal training camp. He was subsequently suspended and fined by the FPF, but he had been expected to return to Portugal for the November international break.

Like Messi, Ronaldo intends to continue his club career with Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia.

#996. Price roars to Grand Slam of Darts title to end four-year major drought

Gerwyn Price defeated Gian van Veen to win Grand Slam of Darts for fourth time; it is Price's first major title in four years; it moves him up to world No 3 above Luke Humphries

Sports Journalist @MegWellensX

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Gerwyn Price picked up his fourth Grand Slam of Darts title with a dominant 16-11 victory over Gian van Veen in Wolverhampton.

The win continues what has been a brilliant 2026 for Price. The Grand Slam marked his fourth major final of the year after making it to the World Grand Prix, World Matchplay and World Series Finals deciders, but this was his first success.

Price also maintained his perfect record in finals at this tournament, adding to his 2018, 2019 and 2021 triumphs.

It is Price's first major victory since 2022. The win also moves him up to world No 3, overtaking Luke Humphries, with Van Veen world No 2.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

With his eighth major win, Price also moves alongside Gary Anderson and Peter Wright in terms of majors won.

Price will now be hoping to continue a four-year-long trend where the winner of the Grand Slam goes on to win the World Darts Championship.

"It's amazing. I've had some close calls this year where I probably should have won games and tournaments, but when it comes along, it's nice," Price told Sky Sports.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"I was probably more nervous in this game than ever. I've lost so many finals and just to keep the media off my back. Now they can stop talking about it and I can go to Minehead next week with a major, so they can leave me alone.

"The sweet thing about this is the last couple of years, whoever won has gone on to win the World [Championship], so...

"If that happens, then I'll take six months out!"

With the Wolverhampton crowd at fever pitch, they were treated to a to-and-fro opening session. It looked like it was all going to go the way of Price when he powered in a sensational 150 checkout for a second break of throw, but Van Veen held his nerve and broke straight back to go into the first break just 3-2 behind.

Van Veen thought he was on for a two-leg cushion in the second session after breaking Price's throw in the ninth leg but, in typical 'Iceman' fashion, Price fired straight back with a 145 checkout on tops to level things at 5-5.

The standard was high and there was nothing separating them.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

While both players were finding some clutch doubling, neither could initially find a strong spell to run away. Van Veen had the first real opportunity to break the throw in the 15th leg but, with both finding trouble down on D2, Price eventually took it to hold and lead 8-7.

Rattling off the next five legs, Price found three breaks of throw and a clutch tops-tops checkout for 100 that left Van Veen without any answers.

In no time, he was three legs away from glory and six legs ahead of Van Veen, his 102.95 average compared to Van Veen's 83.71 for the third session the key statistic.

Van Veen managed to stop the rot with a break of throw but just as he thought he would be able to make it back-to-back breaks, Price took out a clutch 132 checkout on the bull to move 14-9 ahead.

Although Van Veen continued to hold his throw, that was not going to be enough.

The moment arrived at 15-11 and Price decided to win the Grand Slam in some style. With a 118 checkout on tops, his fifth ton-plus finish of the match, Price's crowning moment arrived.

Runner-up Gian van Veen speaking to Sky Sports:

"It has been a very positive week but I am very disappointed. It was a close game and he took out a lot of good finishes. I missed chances.

"I think 16-11 is a flattering scoreline but that's what Gezzy does. He always puts everyone under pressure. He deserved to win."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Sky Sports' Dan Dawson on Price's Grand Slam win:

"Price has had to battle to this title and I think he's had to battle to win this Grand Slam more than he has in any other since his first, because we've seen him play unbelievable stuff to win Grand Slam titles.

"But I think that's what he's had to do to become a winner again, and seeing him smile and seeing that pressure lift, just hearing him talk, I think that is an enormous sign because he's already looking ahead. What can I win next?

"We know that at Ally Pally he is up into No 3 in the world, with Luke Humphries and Luke Littler on the same side of the draw provisionally.

"That game there between Gian and Gerwyn Price, that would provisionally be the semi-final in the other half of the draw.

"So that has done him a favour if he is looking to become a world champion again."

Watch the World Darts Championship at London's Alexandra Palace, live on Sky Sports from December 11-January 3. Stream darts and more through NOW with no contract.

#993. Swing when you’re winning? Biggest leaps across Fifa’s football rankings | The Knowledge

Plus: clubs with roads on their team badges, most and fewest managers per league title, and more

Mail us with all of your questions and answers

“The Scotland men’s team’s highest Fifa ranking was 13th (in 2007) and the worst was 88th place (in 2005) – a difference of 75 positions,” writes Bogdan Kotarlic. “Is this the biggest gap between the best and worst ranking for one national team?”

The gap between Scotland’s best and worst Fifa rankings isn’t the biggest in men’s international football; in fact, Pete Tomlin calculates that a 75-place swing puts them joint 141st with Ghana and Seychelles. And, as Chris Lewis and others point out, there are a couple of other home nations who have had more dramatic swings. Wales and Northern Ireland both moved up 109 places: Wales from 117th to eighth under Gary Speed and then Chris Coleman, Northern Ireland from 129th in 2004 to 20th in 2017.

It is the speed of Scotland’s improvement that was most notable. “At two years, seven months and one day that feels like quite the rise,” writes Robbie Dale. “A look at the data shows it is bettered by only nine other countries. Colombia’s rise from a low of 51 to a high of 12 in exactly two years [between 2016 and 2018] is one notable example. Dominica and Kenya rose up the ranks by 70 and 69 places respectively over the course of just 16 months.”

Some of the biggest movers are countries who joined Fifa after the men’s rankings were introduced in 1992, which means they started at the bottom. “I immediately thought of Bosnia and Herzegovina,” writes JJ Galbraith. “They were ranked 173rd in 1996, shortly after playing their first game as an independent nation. Their pinnacle was 13th place in 2013 – a rise of 160 places.”

That 160-place gap is beaten by only two teams. Kuwait reached 24th in the Fifa rankings in 1998, when they won the Arabian Gulf Cup in style and finished second at the Asian Games. By 2017 they were 189th in the world, a difference of 165 places.

That is 18 places short of the record. “Montenegro were ranked 199th when they played their first international match in 2007,” writes Pete Tomlin. “In 2011 they managed to climb up to 16th, thanks to some strong results in Euro 2012 qualifying (victories against Wales, Bulgaria and Switzerland and a 0-0 draw with England at Wembley).”

Thanks to Pete, Mark Holt, Cameron McGlone, Sean DeLoughry and others for helping us compile this list of the biggest movers.

Pete Tomlin has also crunched the numbers for the women’s game. “The gaps are much smaller,” writes Pete, “due to the fact that the rankings have only been recorded since 2003, there are fewer teams and many of the national sides play very few matches.

“The biggest gap belongs to the Bahamas with a high of 96th and a low of 194th, a difference of 98 places. There are actually two women’s teams with a gap of zero, but this is because they have played so few games. Chad (156th) and Sudan (194th) have never moved.”

“Non-league minnows Plymouth Parkway reached the second round of the FA Cup the other weekend,” writes Jon Archer. “I noticed their club crest appears to feature a road going under a bridge. Are there any other clubs who have roads on their badge?” Indeed the Southern League Premier Division South side have the A38 on their crest, a nod to, erm, the nearby stretch of dual carriageway that helps give the club its name via their former ground at the Parkway Sports Club.

It is not a common occurrence and somewhat depends on how far you want to stretch things. Sunderland, for example, have a section of the Wearmouth Bridge on their crest, which certainly carries a road, though it is not visible. Similarly National League South’s Maidenhead United redesigned their badge in 2020 to celebrate the club’s 150th anniversary – it features a stretch of the town’s Thames river bridge, a nod to where the club played their first game back in 1870, which now carries the A4. Farther afield the German minnows TSG Backnang’s crest features the Murr Valley viaduct, which both overlooks the team’s ground and carries the B14, which links Stuttgart and Nuremberg.

Those might be a bit of a reach, but, far more definitively, across the West Country from Plymouth Parkway are tiny eighth-tier Willand Rovers of the Southern League Division One South. Their badge is a proper old shield effort featuring the River Culm, a castle tower … and the M5 motorway, which slices through the village to the north.

“Manchester United have 20 league titles, won by three managers. Liverpool have 20 league titles won by 10. Which teams have the most and fewest titles won by the most and fewest managers?” asks Will Marquand.

The answers above put Liverpool on two titles per manager and their great rivals down the M62 on 6.66 titles per manager (which is doing Alex Ferguson a great disservice but we have to find a way to make this question work). Daz Pearce offers up one-title-one-manager wonders Leicester (Claudio Ranieri), Nottingham Forest (Brian Clough) and Ipswich (Alf Ramsey) for the most managers per title. We would need a team winning only one title in their history in a season with two different managers to get lower than 1:1 but Dirk Maas has a more impressive example of a team with one manager per title.

“Since the inception of the Eredivisie in 1956, Feyenoord have secured 11 league titles, won by 11 managers: Jiri Sobotka in 1961, Franz Fuchs in 1962, Wilhelm Kment in 1965, Ben Peeters in 1969, Ernst Happel in 1971, Wiel Coerver in 1974, Thijs Libregts in 1984, Willem van Hanegem in 1993, Leo Beenhakker in 1999, Giovanni van Bronckhorst in 2017 and Arne Slot in 2023.” Alex Ferguson’s haul of 13 league titles over his 26 years in the Manchester United dugout makes United’s titles-per-manager ratio hard to beat and, probably, the definitive answer for fewest managers per title. Rangers have won 55 Scottish league titles with only nine managers for 6.11 titles per manager. That is as close as we could get. If you know of a club with a higher number of titles per manager, get in touch at knowledge@theguardian.com.

“It dawned on me recently that if Chelsea were to go on and win the Europa League this year on 15 May that, for a period of 10 days, they would be the holders of both major European trophies (as well as being technically the holders of the Cup Winners’ Cup),” wrote Brian Quinn in March 2013. “Has there ever been another brief period like this when a team held two European honours simultaneously? Perhaps going back to when there were three distinct European competitions?”

Chelsea will indeed claim a unique honour if they triumph at the Amsterdam Arena in May (spoiler alert: they did). Only four sides have ever won different European competitions in consecutive years – Juventus, Milan, Porto and Liverpool – and in each instance the teams were deposed as holders of one trophy before getting their hands on the other.

Milan won the much-missed Cup Winners’ Cup on 23 May 1968, but Slovan Bratislava were crowned the new champions on 21 May 1969, seven days before Milan hammered Ajax in the Bernabéu to win the 1969 European Cup. Similarly Juventus won the Cup Winners’ Cup on 16 May 1984, but Everton won that tournament almost exactly a year later on 15 May 1985, a fortnight before Juventus won the European Cup in a final overshadowed by the Heysel tragedy.

Likewise, Porto fell a week short in 2002-03 and 2003-04 after winning the Uefa Cup then the Champions League under José Mourinho, as did Liverpool between their Uefa Cup and European Cup wins in 1975-76 and 1976-77.

“Ronaldinho played for Ravenna, in Serie C, on Sunday. It was his first professional appearance in more than 11 years,” writes George Jones. “Have any other footballers had long career hiatuses? And has any player had a longer hiatus than 11 years?”

“Against the Netherlands this week, Florian Wirtz scored one goal that went in off a post and one that went in off the crossbar. Has anyone ever gone one better and scored a hat-trick with a goal off each post and one off the crossbar?” wonders David Hagan.

“Seeing Cuba thrash Grenada 9-0 in the Concacaf Nations League, I noted there were eight different scorers (Jorge Aguirre scoring twice). Has any team gone better?” asks Oliver Tuhey.

“My team, Tranmere Rovers, have appeared at Wembley nine times since 1990,” writes David Carruthers. “Can any other team never to have played in the top division beat this?”

“Are Leicester City the quickest team ever to go from winning the FA Cup to playing in the FA Cup first round proper?” asks Ricardio Sentulio.

#992. ‘Pregnancy does not mean game over’: meet the footballers challenging the myths | Moving the Goalposts

Claire Emslie and Emma Kelly are among those taking advantage of new research and guidelines for pregnant players

Claire Emslie wasn’t expecting to be able to run at 81% of her max speed at 32 weeks pregnant.

Emslie, a Scotland international who also plays as a forward for Angel City FC, documented her journey through pregnancy and football training on social media and is part of a growing number of professional female footballers who are getting pregnant in their athletic prime and approaching motherhood with a fresh mindset. Rather than marking the end of a career (notably, Millie Bright announced her pregnancy in September, months after having retired), pregnancy can mark both a continuation and a renewal.

“I think it’s becoming more common. You’re seeing it more often, especially in America,” says 32-year-old Emslie, who trained at high intensity throughout her pregnancy, with a three-person team looking after her. She gave birth to her son, Jamie, in December 2025 and returned to competitive action by May 2026; scoring her first goal since coming back for Scotland in October, and her first club goal this month. “It’s amazing what the body can do. I debunked a lot of myths that I’d heard about being pregnant.”

For many years, says the physiotherapist and Women’s Football Hub founder Carolyn Kent, there was huge caution around high-impact sports and pregnancy. The fear was that overexertion and physical contact – a heart rate going too high, a bad fall, a mistimed kick to the abdomen – could cause miscarriage. But slowly this is changing. In July Fifa launched its Stay in Play guidelines and research, which offer a groundbreaking framework for decision-making around football participation during pregnancy.

“I was always told that once you hit that first trimester, 12 weeks, all contact stops. But actually they’re now saying, no, we need to be a little bit more nuanced than that,” says Kent. The research suggests that while that timeframe should still be considered the loose recommended cut-off point for full-contact football (due to the uterus growing over the pubic bone and offering less protection for the growing foetus in the second trimester), low-contact and modified training can continue in the absence of any medical reason for it not to.

“Pregnancy does not mean game over,” adds Kent. “It does not mean that ‘OK, I’ve got to automatically stop’. That again feeds into this narrative that females are fragile. Your body’s amazing.”

Up to 2021, only 6% of sports science research was done on women, which means gaps are still being filled in. But as the women’s game continues to grow, this is happening at speed, says Sinéad Dufour, a pelvic health physiotherapist and academic who was one of the researchers who developed the Stay in Play guidelines. She gives Fifa credit for recognising the development of the women’s game – its popularity and intensity has soared in the past 10 years with more than six million women and girls playing football in England alone.

“More and more players are now staying through until they’re having families … And they put all this money into research,” she says. They have identified “clear cut” physical and mental health benefits for women to keep up with football, including a lower injury risk postpartum.

“There’s always been a notion that women just aren’t strong and robust the way we actually are, and now the science is proving otherwise,” Dufour says. “I do think some of it relates to the foetus. That’s going to supersede what’s actually good for the woman, right?”

Some of the main considerations players should have, whether professional or amateur, as to whether they should keep playing and training throughout pregnancy, relate to pain, pelvic floor dysfunction, and motor control and movement, she adds. But the decision whether or not to continue playing during pregnancy is ultimately personal.

When Emma Kelly, who plays for Newcastle, unexpectedly became pregnant earlier this year at the age of 29, she was anxious. She had never played with a pregnant teammate before and she had been out for much of the season due to injury. How isolating would the experience be? Was it going to jeopardise her career? “I was questioning whether this is the right time,” she says. “It’s not that I’m ungrateful but it’s just finding it hard being out of the team again and not being able to play the sport that I love.”

Though she continued to train, she and her partner decided she would stop contact football immediately, prior to 12 weeks, as “football is so unpredictable”, she says. As she didn’t want to announce her pregnancy until she was into the second trimester, in the interim she told her teammates that she was unwell. Like Emslie she has been documenting her training with the encouragement of her club and feels as if she is noticing more and more athletes doing the same. “I want to continue as long as my body allows me to,” she says. Her club has been “extremely supportive” with specialised training, physio and equipment.

But for all the newfound positivity around pre-and postpartum for footballers, Emslie says candidly, there are some hard truths that players have to face: namely that pregnancy is a sacrifice. The pitch is their stage and no player wants to be relegated to the role of understudy, relearning how to bend their body to their will. “If I wasn’t worried about [fertility], I wouldn’t have gotten pregnant till I was retired,” she says. “I could have had a full football career.”

The other is that football is a business. “You’re used as a player,” she says bluntly. “As soon as you turn a certain age, or if you’ve got a kid, they look at you different … As a player, you’re wanted until you’re not.” Though she made it clear she wasn’t talking about her own club, which was very supportive of her pregnancy and return, at the time of interview she was two months away from her contract ending with Angel City but had no news of a new deal being offered.

Even so, Dufour says, the body works hard during pregnancy; aerobic capacity is pushed. “The biggest stress test you’re ever going to go through is pregnancy,” she says. Her data shows that some women will achieve personal bests on their return. In short pregnancy could be a secret superpower. In an industry as capitalistic, brutal and data-driven as football, that’s an important fact.

If you have any questions or comments about any of our newsletters please email moving.goalposts@theguardian.com.
