#922. The male footballers best associated with each shirt number – the readers’ edition

Last week we selected 50 players who are synonymous with their squad numbers. Our readers spotted notable absentees so came up with an alternative list, which does not start at No 1 or end at No 50

Which footballers are inextricably linked to their shirt numbers? We picked out 50 players last week who have come to embody the numbers on their backs. It was not an exhaustive list – as our readers have proved. We couldn’t include some legends of the game – Pelé and Lionel Messi for a start – and we missed a few brilliant stories. Thankfully our readers have provided an alternative list. And, creative bunch that they are, they have begun with No 0 and ended with No 51 …

An honourable mention should go to Aberdeen’s No 0. Zerouali is one of the very few to have worn the number (before rules were changed in Scotland). He was a cult hero during a poor time at the club, who died tragically young in a car crash. Lewis

The Manchester City No 1 in the 1940s, 1950s and 1960s. Your article said that Lev Yashin was an automatic choice for No 1. While mention was made of other goalkeepers, there was no nod in the direction of the great Bert Trautmann, the German prisoner of war who became a Manchester City legend. Yashin himself said “my only equal is the German boy at Manchester City”.

Bert’s goalkeeping achievements were many. He only started playing as a keeper in a prisoner of war team before signing for St Helens in the Lancashire Combination League on release from prison. A year later he signed for City, where he made more than 500 appearances as well as playing the last 17 minutes of the 1956 FA Cup final with a broken neck in the days before substitutes were allowed, making important saves towards the end to ensure a City victory. He was also the first goalkeeper voted Footballer of the Year.

Perhaps most remarkable of all, he saved 60% of penalties he faced. Unfortunately, he was not given any international recognition. As a German citizen he could not play for England and could only play for Germany if playing in the country. He would have been a certain starter in the Germany team that won the World Cup in 1954.

He also did as much as anyone to repair British-German relations after the second world war. He went from being booed by 20,000 people on his City debut to being feted by more than 50,000 fans at his 1964 testimonial. He was awarded an honorary OBE in 2004. David Cronin

The greatest living Englishman; the best left-back to have played the game; the best player Nottingham Forest have ever had; and my hero (and Paolo Maldini’s). Will Kitchen

The captain who drove Leeds forwards for well over a decade. Captain of club and country, Bremner was the human personification of Don Revie’s team of the 1960s and 1970s. He had skill, drive, aggression, camaraderie and he played close to (and over?) the line. Thirty years after his early death, he is still the player who Leeds fans hold up as representing the qualities they value in players. It is fitting that the only player to come close to him while wearing the white No 4 was another diminutive, copper-haired Scotsman, Gordon Strachan. As the wee Scotsman with the statue outside Elland Road said: “Side before self, every time.” Nick Ramage

Stan Cullis, the Wolves manager at the time, converted Wright from wing-half to centre-half. He was little more than 5ft 8in, which suggests he would not be a good fit in the position, but he could jump and time it right. He captained England and was the first footballer in the world to gain 100 caps. He also captained Wolves and led them to some headline victories, most notably against Honved. Most importantly of all: he represents football before 1960, when football was more open, more exciting and more rapid in the transition. Kevin R Cox

He was the greatest ever No 6. If Pelé described him as the best defender he ever played against, how can the Guardian not choose him? He excelled at timing, passing and the ability to read a game. He also inspired West Ham and England with his presence. Tim Evans

There are still a few of us left who had the great pleasure to see the greatest No 7 of all time play, for Blackpool and Stoke City. His return to Stoke in the 1960s rejuvenated a team that had been stuck in the Second Division for a long time and helped put them back where they belonged, in the top flight. Matthews was the greatest No 7 of his day and, I would suggest, of all time. John Heath

I never saw him play but my father extolled his virtues to me. In this day and age when players are well paid, maybe overpaid, there should be a remembrance of those who went before them and created this wonderful game we call football. Nick Johnson

So neither of the two greatest players to play the game, at least in my lifetime, is included. If we are talking about the beautiful game, then either Pelé (my preference) or Messi has to be the No 10. Richard Hirst

Simply one of the best Premier League players this decade. His number 11 was often seen from behind, with the three defenders he was about to bamboozle looking worried in the background. Joe

Keane was the most iconic and influential No 16. In the era of omnipresent Manchester United pundits, it’s easy to focus on the contemporary theatrical Keane playing the disgruntled, unimpressed one in the studio so well. But don’t lose sight of Keane winning duels, covering every blade of grass and spraying un-Hollywood but massively effective balls forward. Think Stadio delle Alpi, the scene where he tamed Zinedine Zidane and mounted a comeback against Juventus that enabled the Treble and all that. Think Lansdowne Road in 2001 when he essentially knocked out the Netherlands from the 2002 World Cup. Does Rodri have a movie with Steve Coogan in it? Michael Craig

While I like Iván Zamorano and his little plus sign, Klinsmann wore 18 for much longer. He won the World Cup and European Championship (as captain) in it. He also decided to continue wearing it when No 9 was available, which Zamorano never did. Jochen

The number was initially forced upon him at Eibar, but he kept it at Valencia because it meant following in the footsteps of Pablo Aimar. He disproved the received wisdom that shorter, “weaker”, technical players who sparkled in the Italian and Spanish leagues would not cope with the physicality of football in England. His tactical intelligence and impeccable technique were emblematic of the change in European football that was becoming impossible for English teams to ignore.

He was one of the key components of Manchester City’s all-conquering team, but he represents more than that: the move to a positional game; conserving and recycling possession as a means of placing pressure on the opponents; building up from the back, enabled by an offensive technical player dropping deep. These innovations would have reached the English game anyway, but his presence provided some initial familiarity with them.

He made 125 appearances for Spain, scoring 35 goals and providing 29 assists. He also guided Real Sociedad into a successful spell in his mid-30s. Toby

His shirt number was retired when he moved to Borussia Dortmund and became, at the time, the most expensive 17-year-old in history. I’ve had the privilege of seeing two of Birmingham City’s greats – Trevor Francis will always be my No 8 shirt – putting seasoned defenders on their backsides or scoring brilliant goals. Francis and Bellingham were, and are, Blues legends. Ribs

The raumdeuter won so much with Bayern Munich. For Germans and younger people, if you think of 25, you think of him. He is a legendary player and great person who deserved a mention. Fionn

It has to be Doncaster Rovers legend James Coppinger. “Copps” has been associated with Rovers for more than 20 years. He joined in 2004 and dazzled on the wing for many years before retiring aged 40 in 2021 after a club-record 695 appearances. He wore the No 26 for the entirety of his career, having originally worn it as an academy graduate at Newcastle United, for whom he came on as a substitute to partner Alan Shearer up front in one Premier League game against Tottenham.

Coppinger is not only famed for his longevity. He scored some crucial goals in the club’s rise up the EFL to become an established Championship side, including a sensational hat-trick in a 5-1 win over Southend that sent the club to Wembley in 2008, when they beat Leeds to earn promotion to the second tier. He also scored the dramatic last-second winner that took the club back up as champions of League One in 2013 away at Brentford.

Coppinger is now a first-team coach at the club under Grant McCann, so continues his strong association with Doncaster, having been a central figure in all of their successes across the past 22 years. Adam

AIK are not my club but the death of Ivan Turina – who died in his sleep at the age of 32 in 2013 – shocked all of Swedish football. He wore No 27 and, for 10 straight years, AIK fans chanted his name in the 27th minute of every game. Even though he was only with AIK for four seasons, the Croatian goalkeeper seemed as if he had been there forever, the way he embodied the AIK attitude: completely unapologetic, fearlessly loyal to his own, giving no quarter to his opponents.

It was Dinamo Zagreb supporters who gave him the chant “Ivan Hooligan” but it was seamlessly taken over by AIK fans. His death came at a very sensitive time as AIK had just abandoned their beloved and historic Råsunda Stadium. He might not be well known internationally but, for those of us who follow the Allsvenskan, No 27 always belongs to Turina. David

Christian Vieri for 32! I can’t believe he wasn’t even mentioned! Unforgivable! Vieri is my favourite player of all time! Domingo

A tragic story of a world-class prodigy being struck down in his prime. The amount of former teammates who continue to wear his shirt number is a tribute to his impact. Jamie

No 37 should really have been Rob Lee. He did not wear the shirt for that long – he was No 7 at Newcastle until Ruud Gullit stripped him of that number – but it was long enough to name his autobiography after it. Josh Brown

Maeda, who is relentlessly wearing the No 38 for Ipswich, had his doubters during his time in Glasgow but his epic finish to last season was a fitting farewell for one of Celtic’s recent greats. A regular for Japan, I hope he can make a success of his Premier League move and warrant a place on your next list. Terence Brown

Anelka will always be the iconic No 39 for me, as someone who grew up watching the Premier League in the 2000s. Goals, sulks, titles; he had the lot. Sorry, Bruno Guimarães. Oliver Hatfield

There is a famous children’s song in Italy that talks about 44 cats (gatti) walking in a line. So the shirt number is a play on words with the player’s surname. He wore it at Perugia and Vicenza. PG

Forrest has spent 16 years at Celtic, where he has played more than 500 games, scored more than 100 goals and won 24 trophies. He has done way more to deserve the No 49 than a good young player at Arsenal. Gerry Stuart

While I understand you had to stop somewhere, and 50 is a nice round number, it’s a shame you couldn’t extend your list to 51, where Willian Pacho has staked a claim for being the best to ever wear it. He’s probably the only notable footballer to opt for that number, but that doesn’t diminish his achievement.

While Ousmane Dembélé is the poster boy for the new, all-conquering Paris Saint-Germain, Pacho was the final piece in the defensive puzzle that allowed that world-class attack to roll through everyone. He somehow manages to combine the positional intelligence and range of passing befitting an old-school libero with the speed and athleticism expected of modern centre-backs. That he’s also a graduate of Independiente del Valle in Ecuador – one of the great, unexpected flowerings of talents in today’s football – makes him even more worthy of note. Kári Tulinius

#921. How Premier League's big six keep getting richer

Ten games into the Premier League season, four of the top five places are occupied by 'big six' clubs.

Only second-placed Brighton, a club with a model which must be the envy of many of their rivals, and Premier League ever-presents Everton, have muscled their way in.

In pure financial terms, it should come as no surprise.

The six biggest clubs - Manchester United, Liverpool, Manchester City, Arsenal, Tottenham and Chelsea - now generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the division's other teams.

BBC Sport breaks down how the finances of the big six have exploded, examines new trends and the impact on the transfer market, and asks how much it really matters.

Companies put their money where supporters are prepared to spend it. It is a simple fact of business in every country, a reality of football's food chain.

In England, Liverpool, Arsenal and Manchester United traditionally dominated viewing figures, column inches, shirt sales and sponsorship.

Over the past 20 years they have been joined by Chelsea, Manchester City and Tottenham.

This group of clubs now generate so much money it is hard to imagine how they can fail in the long term - even factoring in short-term performance issues.

We will use Everton, the only club not in the big six to be in the Premier League since its inception in 1992.

This tells a tale of how even one of the league's founding members can be left trailing well behind.

In 2009-10, the gap in revenues between the big-six average and Everton was Â£120m. In 2024-25, that gap had grown to Â£442m.

In large part it is the boom in international TV rights.

Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool, told BBC Sport that it has attracted companies prepared to pay large sums to be associated with the Premier League's top clubs.

"The big football brand clubs have global fanbases and that makes them very attractive to global commercial partners, especially for sponsorship and front-of-shirt deals," Maguire said.

"You combine that with the fact that the Premier League is broadcast to 190 different countries around the world, and especially the international audiences - that allows the clubs to negotiate very good prices."

Only 10% of Everton's revenue comes from commercial deals, while for the big six it is 45%.

It means Everton, and other clubs in the league, are heavily reliant on broadcast income. It makes up 66% of their revenue.

For Everton at least, this should change following the move to Hill Dickinson Stadium.

But that is unlikely to be enough to stop the gap increasing.

It has taken a few years, but Aston Villa and Newcastle have begun to increase their revenue.

This is largely thanks to the financial rewards of Champions League football.

But even Uefa has created a system which entrenches the position of the biggest clubs.

When the European Super League plan was torpedoed, Uefa created a new financial deal called the value pillar.

This reserves 35% of all Champions League revenues, or Â£713m, for the historically most successful clubs.

At the end of the league phase last season City are estimated to have earned Â£37.9m from the value pillar, Liverpool Â£35.5m and Chelsea Â£33.3m. Newcastle received only Â£13.6m.

The good news for Villa is their coefficient has improved greatly, aided by last season's Europa League win.

Their value pillar is projected to be worth Â£25m this season. But that will still be less than the big six clubs in the competition.

The cards are stacked against an ambitious club - not just domestically, but in Europe too.

Take a look at the financial trend of the big six and one thing becomes noticeable - Chelsea are beginning to fall behind.

In the past two seasons, and for the first time in recent history, the Blues recorded the lowest revenues of the big six.

Not just by a small amount. They were Â£74m behind Tottenham, and Â£200m below Liverpool and Manchester City.

City's matchday income is the lowest, with the club's huge revenues largely due to commercial deals.

City, however, have been found guilty of breaching the Premier League financial rules between 2009-10 and 2017-18, inflating the value by using "sham contracts" with sponsors.

The club deny wrongdoing and have lodged an appealed against the verdict.

Stamford Bridge has a capacity of only 40,000, with no easy scope for expansion. The rest of the big six have grounds which hold at least 60,000.

Chelsea generated an average spend per fan of Â£80 in 2024-25, the second highest in the league after Arsenal.

Yet with 20,000 fewer tickets sold than their big six rivals, Chelsea's total matchday revenues are dwarfed.

"Matchday spend has become increasingly important," Maguire said. "There has been a flatlining of broadcast revenues, especially since 2017.

"As a consequence, clubs have had to look at alternative methods of increasing revenues, especially with costs both on the pitch and off pitch rising so fast."

Matchday revenue has effectively stalled for Chelsea, rising only Â£16m over the past 10 years. United's has grown by Â£69m and Spurs, thanks to their new ground, by Â£85m.

"Chelsea are far more reliant upon player sales," Maguire said. "There is a growing divide because the global appeal is very much aligned with three or four clubs.

"Arsenal have re-established themselves with their progress in the Champions League. Manchester United are a brand in their own right. And Liverpool have expanded Anfield from 44,000 to 61,000, with many of those extra seats having gone to commercial."

Chelsea's successful player trading model has so far limited the impact.

But there are signs that, financially at least, the big six could become the big five.

You might recall that Villa and Newcastle were not fans of the old profit and sustainability rules (PSR).

PSR forced both clubs to sell some of their best players to balance the books.

That has changed this season with squad-cost ratio (SCR).

There is a key difference with SCR, in that it allows a club to spend the money they generate on players. PSR limited losses so was more restrictive.

"This does make it a little easier for the likes of Villa and Newcastle to spend money," Maguire said. "But it is still heavily weighted in favour of the big six.

"SCR is different to PSR rather than better. For some people, change is advantageous. For others, it isn't."

The big six generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the other clubs. So they can spend hundreds of millions of pounds more on their squads.

This makes the big six even more powerful in the transfer market.

"Look at the clubs who voted against SCR - Brighton, Brentford, Bournemouth, Crystal Palace, Fulham and Leeds," Maguire said.

"It's very noticeable that those clubs have traditionally been very good at player sales, while they have tended to have lower matchday and commercial revenues."

Most of the big six - the outlier being Chelsea - are not remotely close to the Premier League's 85% SCR limit.

If you give clubs more money to spend on transfers, the likelihood is they will do just that. And the numbers back that up.

Premier League clubs spent Â£3.5bn - not only a highest total for a summer window, but it almost smashed the record for a whole season, the Â£3.53bn set in 2025-26.

The annual accounting cost of previous transfers, or amortisation, has been rising year on year.

"Over the course of the last decade, transfer amortisation has more than doubled and close to tripled," Maguire said.

"Which means that on average, clubs in the Premier League are now spending, or now have a cost which goes into their SCR calculations of just under Â£100m."

Uefa fears that SCR will make matters worse, and have an inflationary impact across Europe.

In the summer 13 Premier League clubs broke their transfer record.

Brentford, Brighton, Palace, Leeds and Nottingham Forest all spent more than Â£40m on a player - unthinkable until recently.

So we have learned that the big six have more money than ever, and the gap is so huge it is impossible for any other club to compete with them, financially at least.

And this is an important point: other than Villa and Newcastle, the other clubs are not trying to compete with the big six.

Clubs like Brentford and Brighton have shown that smart models are just as effective as fat wallets.

They sign the potential stars of the future, nurture them and then sell them to the big six.

Football's ecosystem recycles the big-six money through the transfer market.

But it is a precarious business for these other clubs.

"The smaller clubs have to get it right on a more regular basis than the bigger clubs," Maguire said.

"The big six can afford to make signings which are Â£60m and Â£70m, who turn out to be relative flops, and still have those players on high wages for several years."

And this is perhaps the key point about the vast finances of the big six.

The commercial power of the big six does not guarantee success. After all, United sit in the relegation zone.

Yet Mauricio Pochettino, their new manager, may well get the chance to revamp the squad despite the club spending Â£945m on players in the past five years.

The richest clubs can try to spend their way out of trouble. Again and again.

But the rest of the league are only a couple of bad transfer windows from catastrophe.

And that is the real gap between the big six and the rest.

#920. ‘When I walked for Burberry I met Kanye West’: the two lives of Bromley footballer Omar Sowunmi

Full-time defender and part-time model, the 31-year-old is happy to shine a light on both sides of his dual career

“I was walking down the street one day and someone came up to me and said: ‘I think you should be a model,’” the Bromley defender Omar Sowunmi says. He was already living out many people’s dreams as a professional footballer but was able to assume an alter ego in the world of fashion. There are few parallels between the grind of lower-league football and Milan fashion week but the 31-year-old is adept in both worlds.

Sowunmi’s dual career mixes trips to Doncaster with visits to Paris. On Saturday Bromley travel to Reading under their new manager, Karl Robinson, as they attempt to move off the bottom of League One and the centre-back is clear where his focus lies even after his chance encounter with a model agency employee expanded his horizons.

“I’d get asked to go to a job or I’d even get booked for a job and they’d be like: ‘Oh, we want you to come to Germany for three days,’” Sowunmi says. “But I had to say: ‘I can’t do it, my priority is football.’ As fun and different as [modelling] is, it’s not my main job. Football was my priority and is my priority.

“It’s wicked, the stuff I’ve done modelling. Going to Milan fashion week, being taken to Paris fashion week with brands like Christian Louboutin is a level that I never thought I would reach or be possible when I first started it. Some of the people I’ve met doing it … when I walked for Burberry I met Kanye West … just celebrities and people that I grew up listening to and I feel like without that it probably wouldn’t have happened.”

Sowunmi takes the Nobu Pilates with teacher Marsha Lindsay class twice a month in the five-star hotel of the same name in central London. He is an imposing presence at 1.98m (6ft 6in) tall and grimaces through the session as his muscles are put to the test to keep him in shape for both his professions. It helps him to battle robust strikers and appear on social media as part of modelling campaigns. “Two days ago one of my current coaches said: ‘You popped up wearing a coat on my Instagram the other day. Can you get me one?’” Sowunmi says. “But I had to explain that it doesn’t really work like that.”

Sowunmi’s career path since he left his first club, Ipswich, without making an appearance has been that of a true lower-league player, taking in spells at Yeovil, Colchester and – between two stints with Bromley – Sutton. On the catwalk, he has rubbed shoulders with some of the biggest names in the industry while promoting designer brands and plans to continue doing that once he retires from the day job. He uses social media not only to post videos and images from photoshoots but to show the reality of life as a footballer.

“The fans and everyone that watches you on Saturday or Tuesday or whatever day you’re playing, they get to see you for 90 minutes and they don’t see the full dedication that goes into being a professional footballer,” Sowunmi says. “We’re away from our families for two days [for away games]; we’ll train on the Friday then leave, maybe have a seven-hour coach journey. We’ll have stuff to do at the hotel, stretching sessions, pool sessions, nutrition. We’ll wake up and we’ll have more stuff to do and it’s that whole buildup that I kind of want to show them and give them an insight into what we do.”

Last season Sowunmi helped Bromley gain promotion to third tier for the first time. The step up has been difficult, costing the long-serving manager Andy Woodman his job. “It’s been tough, as you can tell by the league position,” Sowunmi says. “It’s a completely different league. It’s taken a lot of the players by surprise, the difference between League One and League Two, but we’re grinding, we’re working hard and I’m sure it will turn for us.”

A carefully curated moustache sits atop Sowunmi’s lip to raise money for Movember. He is speaking at a charity event on Wednesday to highlight the importance of mental health, a subject close to his heart since his best friend took his own life. “It’s something that is really deep in my heart just being a voice for people and trying to help make a difference in any way that I can,” Sowunmi says. “I was actually on an away trip and I received a call from his dad to give me the news.

“Everyone was asking me what was wrong on the bus and that I wasn’t really speaking to anyone and then I think when we got home it was a four-, five-hour journey. The manager took me to the side and got me to open up to him a little bit. Looking back that actually helped a lot, so I thought if I can help someone to speak to someone or know that it’s fine to speak to someone then I’m definitely here for it.”

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The Original Article was published on 24 June 2026

Retraction to: Nature https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10702-5 Published online 24 June 2026

The authors retract this article, following a suggestion from the editors. Shortly after publication, a preprint (subsequently published (see ref. 1 below)) by Till Sawala identified an inconsistency in our analysis. Our calculations were erroneously comparing the comoving distance between the observed galaxies to the luminosity distance between galaxies in the simulated mocks. Correcting these issues reduces the discrepancy between the observed and simulated samples to 1.48–2.75 sigma, depending on the sample construction. This falls below the standard significance threshold of 3 sigma in the cosmology literature.

Despite the revised uncertainties, our method remains valid and provides tentative evidence for anisotropy in the large-scale distribution of galaxies in the Universe. The revised paper, with corrected uncertainties, will be submitted to another journal. This retraction will contain a link to the new publication, if and when it is published.

#918. Pochettino needs New Manager Bounce to break torrid Manchester United turnover | Jonathan Wilson

Latest hire will depend on fresh faces and time to bed in at Old Trafford where the dugout churn is hardest to budge

Everybody knows the pattern. Performances fade. Results falter. A title challenge becomes clinging on for the last Champions League spot becomes mid-table. Or a promising start becomes a troubling dip, becomes a full-on battle against relegation.

Fans begin to grumble. The media wonder whether the spark has gone. Players look disaffected. A dressing room, once lost, is seldom rediscovered, and few managers are given the opportunity to find it again. A crisis in football, once acknowledged, is only ever resolved in one way: by the sacking of the manager.

With hindsight, Michael Carrick’s dismissal was probably inevitable from the moment Manchester United lost at Hull on the opening weekend, just as Ruben Amorim was doomed from the moment cameras picked him up fiddling with magnetic counters on a tactics board in the rain at Grimsby. The message for Mauricio Pochettino is clear: don’t go playing badly on the east coast.

It’s generally acknowledged that Carrick, while he may not have been the ideal manager for United, was a long way down the list of the biggest problems at the club. So what was the point of sacking him? As Pochettino begins his United career at Anfield on Sunday, what realistically can any manager hope to achieve?

Sackings have become almost ritualistic. Football demands blood sacrifice. How else can the harvest be guaranteed but by the torching of the wicker man? How else can Crystal Palace stay up but by the sacking of Pierre Sage? Once, when the manager defined the club, bought the players, decided the tactics, set the mood, that perhaps made sense. When managers were messiahs, it requires only a slight tweak to the underlying theology to see a logic in sacrificing them.

But managers now, at least at the majority of Premier League clubs, are part of a wider structure. In one of his meltdowns at Spurs, Antonio Conte made the point that it made little sense for him to be answering questions about the broader future of the club when he had so little power compared with the tiers of executives. Why sack the manager rather than the head of recruitment or the sporting director or the chair?

The answer to that perhaps goes back to the emergence of the English idea of the manager, which began in the 1930s and blossomed in the post-war golden age of Matt Busby, Bill Shankly, Don Revie and Brian Clough. As Barney Ronay argues in The Manager, at least part of the reason he became a figure of such pre-eminence was that it was useful for the board to have a hapless ashen-faced figure standing out on the touchline to take the blame. A handful of geniuses aside, the manager was essentially a convenient scapegoat.

But does the sacrifice work? It was one of the shibboleths of football’s early data wonks that the new manager bounce was a myth. What was being witnessed when form improved after a sacking was nothing more than regression to the mean. Which sounds sensible: squads make games and are determined by finance. There is a wealth of evidence that the biggest single factor in determining league position is the wage bill.

And yet there is also evidence that new manager bounce does exist. A lot of early data analysis in football ignored the fact that those involved are human and respond emotionally to circumstance. More recent studies, though, suggest that, while around a quarter of clubs experience no improvement, the first five matches under a new manager show a 41% improvement in points per game, although the impact wears off after around 10 games.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

That feels intuitively true and is readily explicable. A manager under pressure can become embattled, lashing out at enemies real and imagined, their capacity to make lucid decisions impaired as confidence ebbs, creating a doom spiral. Replacing him breaks that pattern and permits a psychological reset.

In a world where everything is studied endlessly, a new manager should make a team less predictable. It’s possible, of course, that as those early analyses suggested, performances would have turned anyway as part of a regression to the mean, but it is curious how often the uptick in form coincides with the replacement of the manager.

Anthropologists are yet to determine precisely why United sacrifice managers so frequently, although there does appear to be some sense of deflecting blame. There is also a sense that it has become routine, that reasons that once probably did exist have been forgotten over time.

Sacking the manager is just what the club do a few months into the season, the ritual now as divorced from its original purpose as modern Hallowe’en customs are from their origins in the Christian commemoration of All Hallows’ Eve.

Will the arrival of Pochettino help? He is a far more ebullient and charismatic figure than Carrick, whose status as a dead man walking for most of this season perhaps meant players did not take him as seriously as they might have an incumbent who appeared to be there for the long term, or had them beginning to ponder moves away from United.

But this remains a mismatched hotchpotch of a squad assembled over six previous managers. If there is some style of play that would suit most of them it has yet to reveal itself.

It will take time for Pochettino to instil in a side that are habitually outrun the levels of conditioning that characterised his Tottenham, and perhaps even longer to get them playing in a coherent pattern. There will probably have to be five or six new signings (and at least as many departures). Probably most difficult of all, there is the entire culture of the club to overhaul, which may not be possible without a change of ownership.

Given United came back from two goals behind three times in their final two games under Carrick, these are not usual circumstances: beleaguered managers rarely inspire such defiance, and the fans never turned against him. In that sense, there will not be the immediate benefit that comes when toxicity is removed.

Some sort of bounce, though, is probable under Pochettino, if only because a negative pattern has been broken. The question is how long it can be maintained.

#917. Will Infantino feel he's already won as Fifa challengers confirmed?

Gianni Infantino has been president of Fifa since 2016 and is standing for re-election for a third time

Philippe Diallo and Kozo Tashima will take on incumbent Gianni Infantino in next year's Fifa presidential election.

World football's governing body has confirmed the three candidates for the election, which will take place at the Fifa Congress in Morocco on 18 March.

European football's governing body Uefa only identified its candidate Diallo fewer than 48 hours before Wednesday's deadline.

French Football Federation (FFF) president Diallo, 63, received the unanimous support of Uefa's executive committee.

Japan Football Association honorary president Tashima, 68, announced his intention to stand against Infantino, 56, earlier this month.

Tashima is a member of the Fifa Council and a former international footballer and coach.

Former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega had also said he intended to stand but was not named as a candidate by Fifa on Thursday.

A late and surprise choice, Diallo said: "I have the experience, the convictions and the values which offer a credible alternative...I'm entering this campaign not just to provide a different voice, but to win."

But he is not the Frenchman some believe Uefa really wanted, as it tries to remove Infantino in the wake of his failed plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

Senior figures in European football had hoped to persuade Arsene Wenger - Fifa's head of global development - to stand against his own boss. Some felt that only he possessed the credibility to pose a serious threat to Infantino's plans for a fourth term.

But after the former Arsenal manager chose not to proceed, Uefa had no choice but to seek an alternative.

So just how credible a challenger is Diallo? Does Infantino's position appear unassailable? And how could he still be stopped from winning another term?

FA explored legal challenge to Infantino staying on

Wenger decides not to challenge Fifa chief Infantino

Japan's Tashima to stand against Infantino for Fifa presidency

An administrator who has worked in French football since 1992 and became FFF president in 2023, Diallo is not a household name. But he has already shown he is prepared to stand up to Infantino.

In September, Diallo claimed he had "seriously damaged the image and unity of football", and said "trust has been broken" over the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) sell-off plot.

According to Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister, Diallo is a "candidate who can instigate real, meaningful and lasting reform" within the governing body.

"We've always made it very clear that our objectives and motivations are driving culture change. That means wide-ranging, systemic reform of football governance rather than simply the replacement of an individual leader," McAllister told BBC Sport.

"I've known Philippe since we were both elected to Uefa's executive committee, and he's an intelligent, honest, sharp-minded football person with an impressive experience of governance in one of the world's football power-houses. Most importantly, he is a person of integrity... Philippe is a fantastic advocate for the change agenda that football needs, and I know his campaign will reflect that."

Infantino remains the favourite to win a majority of the 211 votes, and is thought to have the support of most of Africa (54 members), Asia (47) and South America (10).

However, Uefa hopes that Diallo - whose father was a Senegalese boxing champion who represented France in the 1960 Olympics - could enjoy support in parts of Africa and beyond. He claims he already has the backing of countries beyond Europe.

Laura McAllister is a former captain of the Wales women's football team

While most of Europe's national associations are expected to vote for Diallo, it is clear that he was not Uefa's first choice. "I wasn't initially a candidate, but the insistence of my European colleagues led me to accept the offer," he admitted.

Uefa only approached Diallo about standing in the past week, and senior officials at some European national associations have also told BBC Sport they are frustrated with the failure to find a higher-profile candidate sooner.

Speaking anonymously, one said they only learned about Diallo's potential candidacy on Sunday, and that while they were supportive of him, "it would have been helpful if we'd had someone much earlier" and "a lot of eggs were put in the Wenger basket."

They also made the point that Diallo was yet to publish a manifesto, and questioned whether he could really win.

Another expressed similar sentiments, saying Diallo was a good man, but "not seen as a heavyweight". They claimed that Uefa had "lost the momentum. The process hasn't been great. I really hope they've got a rabbit to pull out of the hat."

McAllister is optimistic: "I have no doubt whatsoever that we will collectively mount a powerful campaign with the objective of winning the election next March". she said.

"The really critical period comes next, once candidate nominations close and eligibility checks are complete."

Despite high-profile critics like Germany manager Jurgen Klopp - who this week said "the opinion is unanimous that a change would make sense" - Infantino does appear to be in a position of strength.

As recently as August it all seemed very different. Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour strongly criticised Infantino for the FFE scheme, while a senior adviser, Carlos Cordeiro, resigned. The heads of three confederations - Uefa, the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf, which runs the game in North and Central America - then signed a letter accusing the Fifa president of breaking trust "through deception".

Amid an increasingly acrimonious civil war, Infantino seemed vulnerable. But the revolt against him then suffered a series of setbacks.

First, Fifa's executives backed Infantino at a crunch meeting in Rabat. Uefa then called off a threatened boycott of Fifa competitions, while potential rivals such as Concacaf chief Victor Montagliani decided not to stand. Aleksander Ceferin chose to stay for a fourth term as Uefa president rather than challenge Infantino directly.

Meanwhile, Infantino's position as the incumbent enabled him to embark on what has appeared to be a world tour, shoring up support. His chances of re-election received another major boost when he proposed to increase the amount of money handed out by Fifa for football development across the world by Â£2.6 billion.

Sheikh Salman, the head of the Asian Football Confederation, then performed a U-turn, endorsing Infantino, who soon after told the BBC he had the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football.

"I'm a professor of politics so I never assume that there's a runaway favourite to win any election", insists McAllister.

"There are plenty of twists and turns to come in this story between now and the election at Fifa's Congress next year.

"This is about structural change and a commitment to modernising the way in which football is governed so it benefits all who play and watch...that imperative will remain and we will hold the new president accountable for much-needed change."

"The current weaknesses of global football governance have been brutally exposed of late. This has helped coalesce and unite opposition to Gianni Infantino, but also to articulate the widely-held demands that things must change."

So with just four months until the presidential election, where could Infantino still run into difficulties?

Litigation is arguably the most obvious. As part of its wider plan to remove Infantino, Uefa has filed court documents in the US, which includes a potential criminal complaint against him in Switzerland for alleged financial mismanagement.

The legal action has not yet appeared to trouble him. But some senior figures in the European game remain hopeful it could still force Fifa to hand over evidence related to FFE that could prove damaging to Infantino's re-election prospects.

There is pressure from elsewhere in football. Fifa has already agreed to make "key documents" relating to the FFE plan available to members of its council. Infantino's critics believe this disclosure may reveal details that could increase the pressure on him before the election. Last month, the Norwegian Football Federation also submitted a three-part ethics complaint to Fifa regarding the awarding of a Peace Prize to US President Donald Trump, the Folarin Balogun case at the World Cup, and the FFE plot.

The Democrats' victory in the US midterm elections means scrutiny from beyond the sport too. Earlier this year, Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee launched an inquiry into Infantino's ties with Trump. In September, a spokeswoman said FIfa's co-operation with the investigation had been "woefully inadequate." But armed with extra powers, they could now force him to hand over relevant documents or give evidence.

Recent months have also seen a series of potentially damaging stories emerge in the media about various aspects of Infantino's leadership. So far they seem to have done little harm to his re-election chances, with Fifa claiming "it is evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine [him]". But the scrutiny is likely to continue.

With uncertainty over how much support Tashima will have, it seems Diallo is the challenger most likely to test the strength of Infantino's supporter base. There is a danger that the vote against Infantino is split.

It has not gone unnoticed at Fifa that as recently as March, Diallo was quoted congratulating Infantino when the Fifa president visited Paris, external to highlight a mini-pitch programme and the need for more football infrastructure globally.

A lot has changed since then, however. And now the Frenchman has been tasked with finding a way of unseating Infantino, and becoming just the 10th Fifa president in its history.

#916. Summer signings join Lionel Messi among MLS’s top earners: Takeaways from the league’s salary release

How much in player salaries did it take to earn a point in the 2026 MLS regular season? The latest batch of salaries lends some insight

Lionel Messi has closer company at the top of MLS’s list of highest-paid players, thanks to another pair of former Barcelona attackers. The Inter Miami captain is still comfortably the league’s top earner, on a guaranteed compensation of $28.3m. Robert Lewandowski (Chicago Fire) and Antoine Griezmann (Orlando City) have entered the list with the second and third highest wages, while Atlanta United’s Breel Embolo, another summer signing, ranks fifth on a guaranteed compensation of $10.8m. Second-year LAFC forward Son Heung-min sits fourth on $11.2m.

Casimiro, who joined Messi in Miami at the end of his contract with Manchester United, is his team’s fourth top-earner with a guaranteed compensation of $3.54m. This comes after Miami announced his signing as a non-designated player to the surprise of some as the Brazilian arrived on a Bosman transfer rather than a loan-with-purchase, as Rodrigo De Paul had last summer, to keep Miami rules compliant. The MLS Players’ Association lists Casimiro on a base salary of $896,004.

All of these earnings figures were revealed as part of the MLS Players’ Association’s twice-a-year data dump, with the latter installment dropping hours before the league’s postseason commenced. While these figures don’t include transfer fees and therefore don’t tell the whole picture of a team’s investment in its roster, it’s a useful bit of insight in regards to how each team is spending on player wages.

Figures are players’ guaranteed compensation inclusive of base salary and all guaranteed bonuses; does not include marketing and other bonuses.

Thirteen of MLS’s 30 clubs have a new highest earner after a busy post-World Cup transfer window. Two – Anders Dreyer (San Diego, $3.6m) and Mateusz Bogusz (Houston, $2.5m) – rose to the top after the departure of a higher-paid teammate. Lozano overtook the injured Riqui Puig after arriving with the LA Galaxy on loan from San Diego. Lewandowski, Griezmann, and Embolo hold similar status, while Charlotte replaced Wilfried Zaha with Allan Saint-Maximin ($7.2m) earning nearly three times as much as the Crystal Palace great.

Other top-earners signed from beyond the league are Brais Méndez (Columbus, $5.2m), André Luiz (Kansas City, $3.3m), and Kai Wagner (Philadelphia, $1.6m). Two strikers who were traded within the league mid-season signed fresh terms that made them their new teams’ highest-paid players: Rafael Navarro (St. Louis, $4.95m) and Dejan Joveljic (Seattle, $3.7m).

The standout failure of the new big earners is Alexis Sánchez. The 37-year-old Chile legend came to North America this summer, joining CF Montréal and making 15 league appearances for the Quebecois club but failing to register a single goal or assist. His $2.97m guaranteed compensation makes up 24.6% of the team’s wage bill.

Griezmann’s arrival means that Messi no longer carries the largest share of any team’s wage bill, as Orlando has dedicated slightly more to the Frenchman (49.5%) than Miami has to the Argentinian (47.7%). Lewandowski narrowly trails by accounting for 47.3% of Chicago’s wage spending. Importantly, Messi’s contract includes add-ons; a portion of Apple TV subscriptions, merchandise sales through Adidas and Fanatics, and an optional ownership stake in Miami when he retires.

Other notable new wages include former Middlesbrough attacking midfielder Morgan Whittaker (Colorado, $2.0m), former Watford and Everton midfielder Abdoulaye Doucouré (Charlotte, $1.0m), former Manchester United left-back Tyrell Malacia (Cincinnati, $1.04m), former NYCFC playmaker Santi Rodríguez (Columbus, $3.9m), South Africa striker Lyle Foster (Houston, $1.8m), former Celtic striker Kyōgo Furuhashi (LA Galaxy, $1.1m), Tunisia winger Elias Saad (Nashville, $1.7m), former Leeds winger Jack Harrison (New England, $3.65m), Côte d’Ivoire winger Bénie Traoré (NYCFC, $2.5m), former Netherlands striker Vincent Janssen (Portland, $1.75m), Tunisia winger Elias Achouri (San Diego, $2.6m), Scotland goalkeeper Angus Gunn (San Jose, $1.6m), and Southampton loanee Damion Downs (St Louis, $1.6m).

While this exercise cannot confidently include every transfer fee paid, the timing of this year’s drop after the regular season’s end allows us to size up how teams spent on wages against the league table.

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

Does spending more equal success? There’s a degree of correlation there, but it’s not strong.

How valuable is it to get a point in MLS? In 2026’s wage economy, exactly $512,394.

#915. Why Nvidia CEO's affair with alleged Chinese spy matters for AI race

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has apologized for an affair with a woman the US believes was spying for China. The story could have profound implications for the world's most valuable company and the global AI race.

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's admission to an affair with a woman whom US intelligence officials believe was working as a spy for China could have profound implications for the $5 trillion (€4.47 trillion) company.

The Financial Times first reported on Huang's affair with Alice H., an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of Nvidia, which has been suspected of trying to circumvent export controls to get advanced Nvidia chips into China.

The newspaper reported that the US government and its intelligence community believe she was recruited as a spy by China's Ministry of State Security intelligence agency.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

US government officials drafted a memo about the allegations shortly before US President Donald Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping in May.

Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese spy has exposed him and the company to criticism that it may have allowed China to obtain valuable trade secrets as Beijing tries to gain an edge in the race to develop advanced AI models.

Nvidia is initiating an investigation led by independent board members and an external law firm. It said in a statement that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort."

"The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders," the company said Sunday. "While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board's inquiry will examine all available information."

The company's shares fell in early trading on Monday.

While US intelligence officials have not commented publicly on the claims, Trump — with whom Jensen Huang has a close relationship — has backed the Nvidia boss.

"He's an honorable guy," said Trump. "I have not spoken to him ​about it. I just know he's a ​fine person, but you never know what is going on. I hope everything's fine."

Tim Culpan, an Asia tech reporter who has covered Nvidia and Huang closely for years, told DW that while Nvidia's fundamental strengths as a company remain in place, Huang is hugely personally damaged by the story.

"They're still going to make great chips and they're going to sell them to millions of customers around the world who want the best AI chips in the world," he said.

"His opinion is going to carry a lot less weight now. And that, in the long term, will flow through to Nvidia and Nvidia's own corporate interests. So it won't be immediate. It's really a fact that he doesn't have the sway or the power that he might have had one week ago simply through this."

Richard Windsor, a tech analyst and the founder of research company Radio Free Mobile, said the news could be very serious for Nvidia given how much the company has revolved around Huang for decades.

"This problem is particularly acute because Jensen Huang is very hands-on, meaning that the key decisions that led to its success were ultimately taken by him and because there is no obvious successor," he said.

"I suspect we are about to find out just how much the market thinks that the company is dependent on its iconic founder and CEO."

Nvidia and Huang's attitude toward China and potential Chinese customers has been a bone of contention with US intelligence officials — despite Huang's close relationship with Trump.

Huang has repeatedly lobbied Trump to ease restrictions on the sale of Nvidia chips to China. A 2025 export control deal heavily curbed sales, but Trump subsequently permitted the export of older H200 Nvidia chips to China in return for the US government receiving a cut of the sales.

However, that deal has been complicated and bogged down by Washington's strict export-license review. China has also initiated import controls, despite strong demand from Chinese companies. China lacks access to the most advanced AI-capable chips. Beijing wants to develop its own alternatives but has struggled to catch up.

Huang has argued that Chinese dependence on Nvidia's chips would prevent rivals such as Huawei from catching up and boosting China's ambitions to dominate AI supply chains.

However, that argument has been dismissed by many US intelligence officials. They fear that unlimited Chinese access to the most advanced Nvidia chips would boost China's domestic AI sector, lead to its AI models catching up with the leading US models and see the chips being used in Chinese military applications.

The US-China rivalry has become a central theme in the global AI story, with both countries seeking to gain an upper hand in the technology. Leading US AI executives such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei have argued that US AI companies can't afford to take a prolonged pause to allow safety standards in AI to catch up, if they're going to prevent Chinese firms from gaining an advantage.

Washington's central fear over Huang's affair is that it could have led to Beijing obtaining vital trade secrets or other key information about how Nvidia makes its most advanced chips.

Windsor thinks Huang will survive the "severe test" due to his importance to the company. He also cast doubt on the extent to which Beijing and its leading tech firms have learned from Nvidia's chips, pointing to China's own chip ambitions and commitment to have its firms buy its own semiconductors.

"I am far from convinced that Chinese AI has materially benefited from technology or illicit chip imports that it gained from Nvidia," he said.

The news comes at a particularly challenging moment for Nvidia, which has benefited massively from the AI boom thanks to its position as the leading maker of cutting-edge semiconductors needed for AI applications.

Nvidia's valuation has soared dramatically in recent years as companies rushed to buy its chips, becoming the world's first $5 trillion company in October 2025.

However, doubts over the sustainability of the $9 trillion capital expenditure AI boom have sparked a major sell-off in stocks related to the boom in recent weeks. The Democrats' sweeping victories in the US midterms have added to the doubts, given the strength of voter opposition to data center construction in the US.

#914. Sutton's predictions v world champion boxer Lauren Price

Manchester United start life under new boss Mauricio Pochettino on Sunday but will they get their first Premier League win since August when they face Liverpool at Anfield?

"My worry for United is that they have one of the worst back fours in the Premier League," said BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton.

"Their defensive record is something Pochettino will try to address but, whoever he picks, they are just not very good."

Sutton is making predictions for all 380 Premier League games this season, against AI, BBC Sport readers anad a variety of guests.

For week 11, he takes on boxer Lauren Price, who is an Arsenal fan.

She will defend her unified welterweight titles against Michaela Kotaskova on Friday, and has a shot at becoming Wales' first undisputed world champion after the vacant WBO welterweight title was added to the fight.

Price returns to home soil at the Utilita Arena in Cardiff for a fight that will be shown live on BBC Two and BBC iPlayer, from 21:00 GMT.

Do you agree with their predictions? You can pick your own below.

The most popular scoreline selected for each game is used in the scoreboards and tables at the bottom of this page.

A correct result (picking a win, draw or defeat) is worth 10 points. The exact score earns 40 points.

Want to make more predictions? You can play BBC Sport's new Match of the Day predictor game every week, featuring six fixtures from domestic and European competition.

Price, the first Welsh boxer to be an amateur world champion and win Olympic gold, said: "When I turned pro it was my dream to become 'undisputed'. To achieve that and make history again for Wales on Friday, and in front of my own fans too, would be a dream come true."

Before turning to boxing, Price was a world kickboxing champion and international footballer - she captained the Wales Under-19 side, and played for the senior team as well as Cardiff City.

"My football days have helped me massively to get where I am in the ring today," the 32-year-old told BBC Sport.

"I honestly believe my footwork, and how fast my feet are, comes from when I played football.

"I am really proud of everything I achieved in football, especially playing for my country. It is the same now in boxing - to get in the ring and represent Wales is always an honour."

Price said the support of her grandparents helped her become successful at so many sports - and she followed her grandad, Derek, by becoming an Arsenal fan too.

"When I was a kid I was absolutely besotted with football and Arsenal were THE team when I was growing up," she explained.

"It was just the way they played under Arsene Wenger, and how they passed the ball - it was incredible. I loved Robin van Persie but Thierry Henry was my icon, my hero."

Chris Sutton and Lauren Price were speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

The AI predictions were generated using Microsoft Copilot Chat - we simply asked the tool to 'predict this weekend's Premier League scores'.

The wheels have come off for Enzo Maresca at Manchester City with three Premier League defeats in a row.

It's not just City's results which have been alarming, either - they were well beaten by Nottingham Forest last time out, and their performance would have been the biggest concern for their manager.

In contrast, Fulham's results have improved of late and they are unbeaten in four league games. They've done all right whenever I've seen them this season, so I'm not surprised to see them picking up points.

Still, the international break probably came at a good time for Maresca to sort things out. Erling Haaland is scoring again too - not that he ever really stopped for very long - and I'm expecting City to be much better here.

I'm even going for them to keep a clean sheet, for the first time in eight games. I'm always brave... which is why I am bottom of the predictions table.

Lauren's prediction: City are having a tricky time of it at the moment but they should still win this. 2-0

I was at Sunderland's win over Chelsea and they thoroughly deserved it. They had been on a dreadful run of results before then, but it was a reminder of what they are about.

Brian Brobbey was just phenomenal for the Black Cats in that game but, like his captain Granit Xhaka, he is injured and will miss out here.

That just makes me think Aston Villa will have the edge. I always fancy them at home anyway with the way they go after teams, although I don't think this will be easy for them.

Villa boss Unai Emery was fuming after his side threw away a two-goal lead twice in their 4-4 draw at Manchester United, but they will hold on this time while Sunderland go down fighting.

Lauren's prediction: Villa are going really well. 2-1

Bournemouth have won eight games in a row in all competitions and it is incredible how Marco Rose has turned things around after a slow start.

The Cherries were absolutely flying before the international break - but will the two weeks off affect their momentum?

Forest did not need the break either, after their brilliant win over Manchester City.

That was such an important result for their manager Oliver Glasner but I think they will find it difficult to follow it up at Bournemouth.

Lauren's prediction: Forest shocked City last time out but I am going with Bournemouth here, they are on a brilliant run. 2-1

Chelsea were so lethargic when I watched them lose against Sunderland, and I don't think they were hard done by in that game - they looked flimsy at the back, and were deservedly beaten.

I had a bit of a pile-on from some Chelsea fans for saying that after the game, but then Xabi Alonso came out and was also heavily critical of the way they had defended - so he and I are on the same page there.

If Joao Pedro is fit then they will at least have more physicality up front this week, but I still have a feeling Leeds will get something out of this.

Daniel Farke's side got a great win over Tottenham last time out and they do not give much away - Arsenal and Brighton are the only top-flight teams to have conceded fewer league goals this season.

Leeds have definitely benefited from signing keeper James Trafford and what a move it has been for him personally as well.

I admire him for that, because he could have hung around at Manchester City as Gianluigi Donnarumma's number two, but he wanted first-team football. Now he is battling it out with Jordan Pickford to be England's number one.

Lauren's prediction: I don't think Leeds will keep Chelsea quiet. 3-1

This is the battle of the Franks... Lampard versus Thomas.

Thomas Frank's first conundrum as Crystal Palace's new manager is to stop them leaking so many goals - they have conceded 24 in their first 10 games, which is concerning.

I still think Palace have got some really good players, like Ismaila Sarr, Jorgen Strand Larsen and Jean-Philippe Mateta, and it's just a case of them getting fit and finding some form.

The way Coventry play, the Eagles are going to get some chances - but can they take them?

Frank Lampard's side counter-attack with such vigour, so I definitely think they will score... but I can see Palace's forward players having some joy too.

Lauren's prediction: I'm standing next to a Palace fan now, Ed from Boxxer, so I've got to go with them here! 0-2

We've seen Palace change their manager after making a disastrous start but they are still only four points below Ipswich and they will certainly see that as retrievable.

The Tractor Boys are not in the relegation zone but they are still in a relegation fight so, it is important for them to keep picking points up here and there. The trouble for them is that I don't see them getting anything at Tottenham.

Spurs lost to Leeds last time out but I still think they have turned a corner with their performances before that defeat.

I actually think this will be a routine win for Roberto de Zerbi's side, and I'm going for them to keep a clean sheet too.

Lauren's prediction: Spurs will take this one. 2-1

I am covering this game and I think it is a huge one for Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle.

The Magpies have picked up as many points - 12 - in their first 10 games under Jaissle as they did when Eddie Howe was in charge last season, but I still don't think their fans are overly convinced by him.

Some of their unease is because Newcastle don't seem to have a defined style of play, and can be a bit kamikaze going forward.

Because of that, I just think Arsenal will pick them off, and win comfortably.

The Gunners have conceded only five league goals so far and have made an incredible start to their title defence with nine wins out of 10.

The worry for their rivals is that it feels to me Mikel Arteta's side have not even got going yet, but I still don't see anyone being close to them.

Lauren's prediction: No problems for Arsenal here! 0-4

Hull are going to scrap and fight - they have not won for eight games now, but they have still picked up some points because of their battling approach.

You know they will get in Brighton's faces but I don't think it will bother the Seagulls too much.

I want to apologise to Hull fans because I keep writing the Tigers off every week, but I am going to do it again here because Brighton are such a good team going forward and defensively.

Lauren's prediction: Brighton to edge this one. 0-1

Good luck to Pochettino. I like him as a manager and he seems a decent guy too.

He will need some luck as well, because it is going to be incredibly difficult for him to succeed at Old Trafford.

The constant for Manchester United is their managers keep getting the sack, when the club's problems seem to be deeper-lying than that.

Pochettino will get time because of what he has taken over, but it is amazing and also alarming to think United are in the bottom three, and could be bottom by the time this game is played.

As well as being so poor at the back, they have a midfield without any great athleticism and, stylistically, they did not really have an identity under Michael Carrick.

If you are Pochettino, you are probably going into the dressing room and putting your arm arm around Bruno Fernandes, to get the old sulker onside.

He really needs to, because Fernandes is an outstanding player and played a key role in the club's form with his numbers last season.

United need to see that version of him more than ever now, because so far this season he has not got going at all.

As for Liverpool, well I think they will get there under Andoni Iraola. It is just taking a bit of time for his players to adapt to his style.

They are not particularly fluid most of the time, and it feels like Iraola is not quite sure what his best midfield is.

Liverpool are still a work in progress, and United have picked up some results at Anfield recently - two draws and a win in their past three visits - but I can only see one result here, and it is a home victory.

Pochettino will probably look to defend and play on the counter-attack, and they might get some chances that way, but Liverpool are going to win. The only question is how many they will score.

Carrick began by beating Manchester City and Arsenal in his first two games in January. Pochettino might start by being on the wrong end of a pummelling.

Lauren's prediction: Liverpool are at home and I am going with them to win it. 2-1

Brentford beat Everton 4-2 at the Hill Dickinson Stadium last season but, in three of their past four meetings, the points have been shared.

This has got a draw written all over it, too.

Everton are so solid under David Moyes, and so well organised, that I just don't see them losing. Brentford will keep things tight as well.

Lauren's prediction: Both these teams are doing well and this should be pretty even - I haven't gone for a draw yet, so let's finish with one. 1-1

Before the international break, Chris got four correct results with no exact scores from the 10 games in week 10, giving him 40 points.

His guests were the computer game Football Manager 27 and Miles Jacobson, the studio director of Sports Interactive, the company behind it.

Miles managed five correct results with no exact scores, giving him 50 points, while FM 27 got six correct results with three exact scores, to end up on 150 points.

Their individual totals will be shown on the guest leaderboard below - with FM 27 going top - but they have been combined, giving them an average of 100 points, for the guest score for the BBC predictions league table.

That means they miss out on the weekly win, which ended up in a tie between the BBC readers and AI. They both got six correct results with no exact scores, for a tally of 120 points.

There was only one game where everyone picked the right outcome - Liverpool's 3-1 win over Crystal Palace.

Chris, FM 27, Miles, AI and the BBC readers all backed the Reds to win, but AI was the only one to get the score spot on.

There were two games where no-one got the correct result - Nottingham Forest's win over Manchester City, and Sunderland's victory against Chelsea.

Out of more than 25,000 predictions, fewer than 1,500 people thought Forest would beat City and only 36 of them got the 3-1 scoreline right too.

#913. What history tells us about the Premier League table after 10 games of a season

Past years suggest it is tough to make big positional gains after slow start but that someone now safe will be relegated

The Premier League is about to enter the most intense phase of its season. After 10 rounds of fixtures across the past three months there are 10 in the next seven weeks. Yet if you hibernated for winter, most clubs would be in roughly the same position no matter when in spring you emerged.

Across the past decade, Premier League teams’ positions changed by an average of 2.6 places between matchweeks 10 and 38. Only 5.5 clubs per season moved by more than three places over the final 28 games, with almost half of the teams (89 out of 200) shifting by a single spot at most. Every club other than Arsenal will be looking to improve their position but they need not trouble themselves too much. History shows they will probably finish 2026-27 close to their current standing.

There have inevitably been outliers. Tottenham have tumbled by at least 10 places after matchweek 10 in the past two seasons and Newcastle (in 2021-22), Crystal Palace and Everton (both 2017-18) have risen from the relegation zone at this point to the safety of mid-table by May.

But even moving one position across the remainder of the season can make an enormous difference to a team on the fringe of the Champions League qualification spots, or to those that sit 17th or 18th after 10 games. Not since 2006-07 have the bottom three clubs with 28 matches to go all been relegated.

This fact feels especially relevant this season given two of the three teams in the drop zone have changed their manager since the previous round of matches. Sunderland have stood by Régis Le Bris but he is the favourite to be the next Premier League manager to leave their post. If we can reasonably assume at least one of the clubs currently 18th to 20th will be in the top flight in 2027-28, which is best placed to survive?

It is going to be very tough for Crystal Palace. Opta’s underlying data model implies they are where they deserve to be in the table, whereas Manchester United and Sunderland should be much higher. The largest improvement Palace’s new manager, Thomas Frank, engineered between weeks 10 and 38 at Brentford was two places, which will not cut it this season. Palace have to take inspiration from the 2024-25 season, in which they also had seven points after 10 games yet rose to finish 12th.

Mauricio Pochettino’s Chelsea were 11th going into their 11th game in 2023-24 before ending sixth. As they were also 11th in early April, they made a much shorter dash to the finish line, though. Pochettino’s teams usually improve as campaigns wear on, with Tottenham rising three places after week 10 in each of his first three seasons with the club. A similar lift in his new role would not make this season a rousing success for United but it would stave off the unthinkable idea of relegation.

For someone to escape, someone else must take their place. Ignoring the possibility that the answer to “who?” may be Manchester City, the team in 17th are inevitably the ones most at risk. Of the 13 sides in the past decade who were outside the drop zone after 10 games but went down, six were fourth-bottom going into matchweek 11.

Given that the points gap between first and 20th (20) was last lower at this stage in 2015-16, those figures may be more pertinent than position this season. Leeds in 2022-23 and Bournemouth three years earlier had 13 points after 10 games but were relegated, as did Blackpool in 2010-11 and Middlesbrough two seasons before them.

Only nine clubs are now above that bar, with Aston Villa, Newcastle and Tottenham among those who are not. The table is unlikely to change too much before the end of the campaign but there is a distinct chance that a secure-looking side will perish.
